The category includes certain modest snacks or amenities, but does not excuse recurring substantial or cash-equivalent benefits merely because employees call them perks.

entries.title: IRC §132 — Other fringe categories
entries.summary: Qualified transportation fringes, retirement-planning services and certain on-premises athletic facilities may qualify for specific exclusions.
entries.details: Different statutory limitations and eligible recipients apply; do not assume every benefit can be extended tax-free to family members.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 60
entries.laymanExplanation: Tax law has additional special rules for certain transit benefits, retirement-planning help, and on-premises gyms.
entries.legalExplanation: Section 132 recognizes separate qualified categories including qualified transportation fringes, certain retirement-planning services and on-premises athletic facilities. Each has its own eligibility, recipient, dollar and facility requirements; the source's eight assigned questions test how to identify the correct category rather than apply a generic exclusion.

entries.title: IRC §125 — Cafeteria plans
entries.summary: A qualifying cafeteria plan allows an employee to choose between taxable cash and specified tax-favored benefits without automatic taxation solely because cash was available.
entries.details: Without statutory protection, the constructive-receipt doctrine could tax the available cash choice. Coverage and nondiscrimination limitations apply.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 62
entries.laymanExplanation: A cafeteria plan lets workers choose among specified benefits and cash without making all the qualified benefit choices taxable just because cash was available.
entries.legalExplanation: Section 125 authorizes an eligible cafeteria plan allowing choice of cash versus specified excludable benefits without immediately taxing cash forgone under constructive-receipt rules. Qualified benefits, nondiscrimination, annual elections and use-it-or-lose-it constraints depend on the type of plan and applicable regulations.

entries.title: Constructive receipt
entries.summary: Tax doctrine potentially treating income as received when unrestrictedly made available despite the taxpayer's choice not to take it.
entries.details: The chapter references this doctrine to explain why §125 cafeteria plans need express statutory authorization; full timing rules occur later.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 62
entries.laymanExplanation: You can't always avoid income tax by refusing money that's already available to you. Tax law may treat it as received anyway.
entries.legalExplanation: Under the constructive-receipt doctrine, a cash-method taxpayer may be treated as receiving money that is made available without substantial restrictions even if not physically drawn. The reading uses this doctrine to explain why a §125 election to take nontaxable benefits instead of available cash requires a specific statutory exception.

entries.title: Use-it-or-lose-it rule
entries.summary: Certain cafeteria-plan amounts designated for eligible expenses may be forfeited if not used within permitted periods.
entries.details: The chapter illustrates the planning burden; specific carryover and grace-period exceptions should be checked under current plan rules.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 62
entries.laymanExplanation: Some benefits money must be spent on eligible expenses within set time limits, or you may lose unused amounts, subject to plan exceptions.
entries.legalExplanation: The reading discusses annual cafeteria-plan elections and forfeiture of unused designated dependent-care or health expenses, with specified exceptions for qualifying life-event changes. Do not present the casebook's simplified 'cannot carry over' statement as universally applicable to every modern FSA, which may have permitted grace periods/carryovers under current rules.

entries.title: Employer-provided health coverage — §§105–106
entries.summary: Qualifying employer-paid health insurance and certain reimbursements for medical care can be excluded under specific statutes.
entries.details: The text describes employer-paid medical insurance, medical expense reimbursements, and the role of §125 health FSA arrangements; verify specific statutory requirements.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 63
entries.laymanExplanation: Employer medical insurance and certain medical reimbursements often receive favorable tax treatment under special rules.
entries.legalExplanation: Sections 105 and 106 generally confer exclusions for qualifying employer-provided accident/health plan coverage and specified payments/reimbursements, while dependent-care and cafeteria-plan treatment involves §§125/129. The Chapter 2 discussion contrasts this major tax-favored form of compensation with ordinary wages.

entries.title: Turner v. Commissioner
entries.summary: The court used an amount lower than the stated retail ticket value, recognizing valuation difficulty for the particular benefit.
entries.details: Assigned excerpt: the reproduced court opinion, not merely an incidental citation.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), reproduced judicial opinion, Chapter 2 pp. 65–67.
entries.facts: Reginald Turner won two restricted nontransferable first-class steamship tickets by answering radio-program questions. Their retail price was $2,220; the Turners reported $520. They exchanged their tickets plus $12.50 for four tourist-class tickets to Rio de Janeiro and vacationed with their sons.
entries.issue: What amount must the taxpayer include as gross income from winning restricted cruise tickets whose market ticket price exceeds what the tickets are worth to the winner?
entries.holding: The Tax Court included $1,400 of income from the prize—between the $520 reported and the Commissioner's $2,220 retail valuation.
entries.reasoning: The tickets were not transferable or readily saleable and were a luxury the recipients otherwise would not have bought, so retail price overstated actual value; nevertheless the family obtained real travel, food and vacation benefits. The court made a pragmatic factual valuation based on limited evidence.
entries.rule: A valuable noncash prize is included in income, but unusual transfer restrictions and marketability may affect valuation; precise amounts can be fact-dependent.
entries.exam: Identify a taxable award first, then consider sticker value, restrictions on resale, available alternatives and reliable valuation evidence.
entries.examApplication: Identify a taxable award first, then consider sticker value, restrictions on resale, available alternatives and reliable valuation evidence.
entries.laymanExplanation: Someone won expensive travel tickets they couldn't easily sell. The court did not simply use the full ticket price; it looked at what the benefit was realistically worth.
entries.examTrap: Turner's case-specific valuation does not establish a universal rule that subjective personal value always overrides objective market value.
entries.sourceRole: Week 2 assigned judicial opinion (reproduced in textbook)

entries.title: Why fringe-benefit exclusions exist
entries.summary: Valuation, business purpose, fairness, enforcement cost and historical practice help explain special exclusions.
entries.details: Google employer meals, frequent flyer miles, business entertainment, and valuation debates are optional policy context.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 54
entries.legalExplanation: Noncash fringe benefits raise three policy concerns: fair treatment relative to cash wages, how to value employee benefit when employer purpose or transfer restrictions matter, and practical IRS administration/enforcement. The tech-firm meal article and frequent-flyer nonassertion policy are optional illustrations rather than categorical statutes.
entries.laymanExplanation: Tax-free work perks might be fair or unfair depending on what employees get. They're also hard for the IRS to value and monitor.

entries.title: IRC §107 — Ministers' housing exclusion
entries.summary: Qualifying ministers may exclude specified employer-furnished parsonage rental value or eligible housing allowance, within statutory limits.
entries.details: §107(1) excludes the rental value of a furnished parsonage provided as compensation. §107(2) excludes a qualifying designated housing allowance used for the home, limited by fair rental value including furnishings, related property and utilities. IRS guidance also limits allowance exclusion to the amount designated in advance and actually spent. Housing allowance generally remains subject to self-employment tax.
entries.source: IRC §107; IRS Ministers' Compensation and Housing Allowance FAQ; Gaylor v. Mnuchin (assigned PDF)
entries.elements: Compare the housing allowance officially designated in advance, the amount actually used to provide a home, and the home's fair rental value with furnishings and utilities; subject to qualifications.
entries.examTrap: Distinguish income-tax exclusion from self-employment tax treatment and §107(1) furnished housing from §107(2) cash allowances.
entries.laymanExplanation: A qualifying minister may be able to exclude certain employer-provided housing or a designated housing allowance from income tax, within limits.

entries.title: Gaylor v. Mnuchin
entries.summary: The Seventh Circuit held §107(2)'s clergy housing-allowance exclusion did not violate the Establishment Clause, reversing the district court.
entries.facts: Freedom From Religion Foundation employees and their organization challenged the income-tax exclusion for qualifying clergy housing allowances under IRC §107(2). A district court ruled the exemption unconstitutional; the government and religious organizations appealed.
entries.issue: Did §107(2)'s tax exclusion for clergy housing allowances violate the First Amendment's Establishment Clause, and did the challengers have standing?
entries.holding: The plaintiffs had standing, but §107(2) did not violate the Establishment Clause. The Seventh Circuit reversed the district court's judgment.
entries.reasoning: The court examined the historical tradition of religious tax accommodations, comparable housing exclusions in the Code, secular administrative convenience, denominational neutrality, and avoiding excessive entanglement. Applying then-prevailing Establishment Clause reasoning, including Lemon-related analysis and historical practices, it found the exemption constitutionally permissible.
entries.rule: A legislative tax accommodation for religious housing does not inherently violate the Establishment Clause; Gaylor upheld §107(2) based on its statutory context, religious neutrality, and historical practice.
entries.exam: If challenged tax exclusion for clergy housing, identify §107(2), address standing, apply constitutional limits and distinguish the Seventh Circuit's holding from later Supreme Court changes to Establishment Clause methodology.
entries.examApplication: Analyze whether a qualified minister's designated housing allowance is excluded under §107(2) and, separately, whether the statute itself survives Establishment Clause scrutiny.
entries.examTrap: Gaylor remains an important decision, but do not apply the old Lemon test as the current governing Establishment Clause framework following Kennedy v. Bremerton (2022).
entries.details: This opinion was provided separately as an 18-page Federal Reporter PDF. Its excerpt includes the Federal Reporter headnotes and surrounding cases; the dedicated brief is only for Gaylor v. Mnuchin, not adjacent cases printed on the same pages.
entries.source: User-supplied Gaylor opinion (1).pdf, 919 F.3d 420–437 (7th Cir. 2019)
entries.sourceRole: Reproduced assigned judicial opinion supplied as a separate PDF

legalWarning.label: METHOD UPDATED AFTER 2019
legalWarning.reason: Gaylor's result upholding §107(2) should be distinguished from its use of Lemon-era Establishment Clause analysis. Kennedy v. Bremerton School District (2022) stated that courts should use historical practices and understandings instead of Lemon and the endorsement test.
legalWarning.authority: Kennedy v. Bremerton Sch. Dist., 597 U.S. 507 (2022)

entries.laymanExplanation: A group challenged a tax break for clergy housing. The appeals court said that the statutory exclusion was constitutional; later Supreme Court cases changed the test courts use for these church-and-state disputes.

entries.title: IRC §132 — line-of-business and discrimination limits
entries.summary: No-additional-cost services and qualified employee discounts have line-of-business and, for highly compensated employees, nondiscrimination requirements.
entries.laymanExplanation: A store's discount or airline's free standby seat may be tax-free under special conditions, but a big perk reserved only for top executives may fail the rules.
entries.legalExplanation: Review §132(b)–(c) and §132(j): no-additional-cost services generally relate to services sold to customers in the employer's line of business; qualified discounts are limited by statutory caps; special restrictions apply to highly compensated employees where benefits favor them. Analyze each classification separately.
entries.details: Review §132(b)–(c) and §132(j): no-additional-cost services generally relate to services sold to customers in the employer's line of business; qualified discounts are limited by statutory caps; special restrictions apply to highly compensated employees where benefits favor them. Analyze each classification separately.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, textbook pp. 59–61; Week 2 syllabus-assigned.
entries.examTrap: Do not assume a discount from any unrelated line of business or offered only to officers always qualifies.

entries.title: Frequent-flyer rewards on business travel — IRS nonassertion policy
entries.summary: Announcement 2002-18 states the IRS ordinarily will not assert underpayment solely because of personal use of frequent-flyer miles or similar in-kind promotional benefits attributable to business/official travel, with stated exceptions.
entries.laymanExplanation: If your employer pays for work trips and you later use the airline miles for a vacation, the IRS generally doesn't pursue tax on that personal use under its announced policy. Cash conversions and compensation are different.
entries.legalExplanation: The source discusses the administrative difficulty of valuing and tracking miles. IRS Announcement 2002-18 describes a nonassertion practice for promotional benefits from business travel. It does NOT cover benefits converted to cash, compensation delivered in miles, or tax-avoidance schemes; distinguish administrative enforcement policy from a blanket statutory exemption.
entries.details: The source discusses the administrative difficulty of valuing and tracking miles. IRS Announcement 2002-18 describes a nonassertion practice for promotional benefits from business travel. It does NOT cover benefits converted to cash, compensation delivered in miles, or tax-avoidance schemes; distinguish administrative enforcement policy from a blanket statutory exemption.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, textbook pp. 62–64; Week 2 syllabus-assigned.
entries.examTrap: This is an announced IRS nonassertion policy, not a general §132 exclusion for all points or cash conversions.

entries.title: Unsolicited samples and Haverly — cited authority only
entries.summary: The textbook uses Haverly to illustrate inclusion when a recipient claims a charitable deduction for unsolicited materials previously treated as untaxed.
entries.laymanExplanation: A principal gets free sample textbooks; simply receiving them isn't treated the same as selling them. But donating them and claiming their value as a deduction can change the tax analysis.
entries.legalExplanation: The book describes administrative treatment of unsolicited publisher sample books and cites Haverly v. United States, 513 F.2d 224 (7th Cir. 1975), for inclusion when the recipient donates such books and claims a charitable deduction. Haverly is only discussed/cited, not reproduced as an assigned judicial opinion.

entries.title: Nondiscrimination requirement for excluded fringes
entries.summary: Some fringe-benefit exclusions disallow favorable treatment for highly compensated employees if benefit eligibility or use unfairly favors that group.
entries.laymanExplanation: An employer can't necessarily make an executive-only discount tax-free just by calling it an employee perk.
entries.legalExplanation: For §132 no-additional-cost services and qualified employee discounts, assess statutory nondiscrimination restrictions and definitions; different categories of fringe benefits have different rules. The employer's uniform availability to employees is factually important for some benefits.

The employer's uniform availability to employees is factually important for some benefits.

topics.title: D. Recovery of Capital
topics.description: Basis and capital-recovery doctrine, wagering losses and reimbursements.

entries.title: Return of invested capital is not gross income
entries.summary: Amounts that merely return a taxpayer's capital (tax basis) are not income; gain generally arises only beyond the taxpayer's recoverable basis.
entries.details: Repayment of the same $500 loan principal, or sale of $500-basis stock for $500, produces no gain. Distinguish receipts representing earnings from recoveries of investment.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 68
entries.examTrap: Gross proceeds are not automatically the same as taxable gain.
entries.laymanExplanation: Getting back money you already invested is not a new profit. If you lend $500 and receive $500 back, that principal repayment is not income.
entries.legalExplanation: The recovery-of-capital principle prevents taxing repayment of one's original economic investment as if it were profit. Buying stock for $500 and reselling at $500 yields no gain; receiving $500 loan principal back is not interest income. Determine basis and amount realized for a property disposition.

entries.title: Basis
entries.summary: A taxpayer's unrecovered tax investment in an asset, ordinarily its cost, subject to statutory adjustments.
entries.details: Basis prevents taxing recovery of one's own investment as though it were income. Reference §§ 1011, 1012, 1016 as developed in the course.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 68
entries.laymanExplanation: Your basis is your tax 'starting cost' in property. It matters because you usually pay tax on profit above that cost, not the whole sale price.
entries.legalExplanation: Basis is a taxpayer's tax investment in an asset, normally initial cost under §1012, adjusted as law requires. Basis is allocated when only part of a larger asset is disposed of. Inaja addresses the rare situation where allocating basis to surrendered rights is wholly impracticable.

entries.title: Amount realized
entries.summary: Consideration received on disposition of property, measured under the governing realization rules.
entries.details: In a simple cash sale, amount realized is sale proceeds; gain is amount realized minus adjusted basis, subject to transaction-specific rules.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 68
entries.laymanExplanation: Amount realized is what you get when you sell property, before subtracting the property's tax basis to figure out gain.
entries.legalExplanation: Amount realized includes the cash and other consideration received on a property disposition under §1001, before subtracting adjusted basis. For a simple cash sale, proceeds minus allocated basis equals realized gain/loss. Do not confuse taxable income with raw sale proceeds.

entries.title: Realized gain or loss from disposition
entries.summary: Realized gain (loss) = amount realized − adjusted basis.
entries.details: Simple example: sell stock for $700 with allocated adjusted basis $400 → $300 realized gain. The character and recognition of the result require additional analysis.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 68
entries.examApplication: Always identify adjusted basis before measuring gain, and separate gain amount from recognition and characterization.
entries.laymanExplanation: Sell something for $700 with $400 in basis: the difference, $300, is your realized gain.
entries.legalExplanation: Under §1001 the basic computation is amount realized minus adjusted basis. Example: 100 homogeneous shares purchased for $1,000; sell 40 shares for $700. Allocated basis=$400; realized gain=$300. Characterization, recognition and limitations are separate questions.

entries.title: Allocate basis when part of property is sold
entries.summary: When an asset or acquired block of property is partly disposed of, reasonably apportion cost basis among the interests disposed of.
entries.details: For 100 shares acquired for $1,000, 40 identical shares have $400 allocated basis. For nonuniform land, allocate by relative value rather than acreage alone where appropriate.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 69
entries.laymanExplanation: If you sell only part of something, you have to work out how much of your original purchase cost belongs to the part sold.
entries.legalExplanation: Reg. §1.61-6 generally requires equitable allocation of cost or basis when part of property is sold. Identical shares may support per-unit allocation; dissimilar parcels of land require attention to relative values at acquisition. Inaja is a narrow exception where exact apportionment cannot reasonably be made.

entries.title: Basis allocation
entries.summary: The assignment of a portion of total cost to property or rights separately sold or disposed of.
entries.details: The book contrasts homogeneous stock with wooded and tillable acreage. An impossible/impracticable allocation may warrant special treatment under Inaja.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 69
entries.laymanExplanation: You can't always divide a property's basis simply by the number of acres or shares; what each portion was worth may matter.
entries.legalExplanation: Basis allocation attributes part of total investment cost to the assets or rights disposed of. On a $1,000 land purchase with originally valued wooded acres at $450 and remaining acres $550, selling wooded acres for $700 gives $250 gain. Do not use raw acreage if one portion is materially more valuable per acre.

entries.title: Inaja Land Co. v. Commissioner
entries.summary: The Tax Court treated the net $49,000 as a tax-free return of capital reducing the property's basis, because reliably allocating basis to the affected property rights was impracticable and the payment was below total basis.
entries.details: The supplied text reproduces a judicial opinion, so this is a dedicated case brief.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), reproduced judicial opinion, Chapter 2 pp. 69–70.
entries.facts: Inaja paid $61,000 for land, fishing-club rights and related water interests. Los Angeles diverted contaminated water into the river, causing damage. The city paid $50,000 for a perpetual easement and release of claims; after $1,000 in legal costs, net recovery was $49,000.
entries.issue: Was the $49,000 ordinary income for lost profits, or a capital recovery from surrender of land-related rights, and how should basis be allocated when the easement cannot be measured reasonably?
entries.holding: The Tax Court treated the entire $49,000 as a return of capital reducing basis, rather than taxable income, because it was for easements/property damage and basis apportionment was wholly impracticable.
entries.reasoning: The record did not support lost-profits compensation. Ordinarily the taxpayer allocates cost to property rights disposed of, but uncertain boundaries, river flow and extent of damage prevented a factual cost allocation. Gain cannot rest on pure conjecture; because the payment was below original basis, the court allowed it to reduce basis.
entries.rule: Ordinarily allocate basis on a partial disposition; if allocation is wholly impracticable and a capital recovery is below total property basis, treat it as return of capital reducing remaining basis rather than recognize conjectural gain.
entries.exam: Determine what damages replace; first attempt defensible allocation to rights sold. Only if truly impracticable consider Inaja-style basis reduction. Capital recoveries above adjusted basis can generate gain.
entries.examApplication: Determine what damages replace; first attempt defensible allocation to rights sold. Only if truly impracticable consider Inaja-style basis reduction. Capital recoveries above adjusted basis can generate gain.
entries.laymanExplanation: A landowner was paid for damage and easement rights. The court allowed the payment to reduce property basis because nobody could reasonably assign a precise cost to the rights surrendered.
entries.examTrap: Inaja is a limited exception to normal partial-sale basis allocation, not blanket exclusion for every easement or settlement.
entries.sourceRole: Week 3 assigned judicial opinion (reproduced in textbook)

entries.title: IRC §165(d) — Wagering losses (2026)
entries.summary: For 2026 taxable years, wagering-loss deduction equals at most 90% of wagering losses, capped by wagering gains.
entries.details: The casebook describes an older loss-to-gains offset. Current §165(d), effective 2026, limits the deduction to the lesser of 90% of losses or gambling gains. The book's discussion of sessions and nonprofessional itemizing requires attention to applicable-year facts.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 72
entries.elements: Allowable wagering loss deduction = min(90% × total wagering losses, total wagering gains), subject to other applicable rules.
entries.examTrap: Do not use the textbook's pre-2026 full-loss offset for a 2026 tax-year problem without checking the test's assigned law.

legalWarning.label: 2026 STATUTE CHANGED
legalWarning.reason: The book states gambling losses are deductible up to gambling winnings; for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025, Pub. L. 119-21 changed §165(d) to a 90% allowable-loss formula capped by winnings.

entries.laymanExplanation: For tax year 2026, the book's old rule for gambling losses changed: even if you lose as much as you win, you may not be able to deduct all of the losses.
entries.legalExplanation: Current-law annotation: for 2026 tax years, §165(d) as amended limits gambling loss deductions to 90% of qualifying losses, no greater than winnings; other itemization and tax rules may apply. The printed casebook gives the pre-2026 'up to winnings' rule and explains session netting. Keep the 2026 amendment clearly identified as later law.

entries.title: Basketing / scheduling rules
entries.summary: Rules that allow losses or deductions to offset only income in a specified category, rather than income generally.
entries.details: Chapter examples: wagering losses (§165(d)), capital losses (§1211), passive losses (§469), hobby-related limits (§183), investment interest (§163(d)).
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 72
entries.laymanExplanation: Some losses can only be used against gains of the same kind. Picture separate baskets for different categories of tax items.
entries.legalExplanation: A 'basket' rule limits deductions or losses to income from a defined category. The reading contrasts gambling losses under §165(d), capital losses under §1211, passive activity losses under §469, hobby limits under §183, and investment-interest limitations under §163(d). Each basket has its own mechanics.

entries.title: Gambling session
entries.summary: A grouping concept used in determining amounts won and lost during a related gambling session.
entries.details: The text distinguishes in-session netting from separately incurred losses, particularly for nonprofessional taxpayers who itemize.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 72
entries.laymanExplanation: A gambling session means a defined period of betting. The way wins and losses are grouped can affect tax calculations.
entries.legalExplanation: The text describes how gambling gains and losses may be accounted for by session and tax year, rather than treating every single wager in isolation. The correct tax consequences also depend on gambler status, deduction rules and tax year; do not assume gross wins are always offset by all gross losses.

entries.title: Clark v. Commissioner
entries.summary: The Board ruled for the taxpayer: the $19,941.10 reimbursement compensated for a loss rather than yielding taxable income.
entries.details:
The supplied text reproduces a judicial opinion, so this is a dedicated case brief.

Related syllabus handout: The government's 2018 McKenney appellate brief distinguishes Clark's unnecessary tax overpayment from reimbursement of legally owed tax. The 2020 Eleventh Circuit opinion is separately identified as follow-up research; do not confuse the brief with a court opinion.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), reproduced judicial opinion, Chapter 2 pp. 73–75.
entries.facts: For 1932, Clark's tax adviser mistakenly prepared a joint return and improperly handled capital losses. Had the adviser correctly compared separate returns, the combined tax would have been $19,941.10 less. Clark had paid the resulting tax due on the filed joint return; the adviser reimbursed him that $19,941.10 in 1934, which IRS sought to include.
entries.issue: Was reimbursement by a negligent adviser of avoidable taxes actually paid taxable gross income, rather than restoration of a loss?
entries.holding: No, on the specific facts. The Board of Tax Appeals held the $19,941.10 was a reimbursement for an unrecovered economic loss, not income.
entries.reasoning: Clark, not the adviser, paid the taxes. The payment restored the harm from erroneous advice rather than a third party directly discharging his tax debt. The source's explanatory note makes clear that the old capital/labor rationale is obsolete after Glenshaw Glass, while the narrow Clark reimbursement holding remains relevant where excess tax was actually paid rather than merely a better transaction hypothetically foregone.
entries.rule: On Clark's narrow facts, reimbursement of an unnecessary tax overpayment caused by malpractice can be treated as return of lost capital, where no prior deduction for the overpayment produced a tax benefit.
entries.exam: Distinguish actual excess tax paid (Clark) from a settlement for tax legally owed on a poorly planned transaction (McKenney government's brief); assess whether an earlier deduction existed.
entries.examApplication: Distinguish actual excess tax paid (Clark) from a settlement for tax legally owed on a poorly planned transaction (McKenney government's brief); assess whether an earlier deduction existed.

legalWarning.label: OLD REASONING NO LONGER LAW
legalWarning.reason: The reading expressly states Clark's 'derived from capital or labor' rationale is no longer good law after Glenshaw Glass, though its narrow reimbursement holding remains.
legalWarning.authority: Glenshaw Glass; textbook's Current Legal Status of Clark note

entries.laymanExplanation: An accountant's mistake caused a taxpayer to pay more tax than legally necessary. The accountant paid him back. The court treated that reimbursement as making him whole, not extra income.
entries.examTrap: Clark's old 'derived from capital or labor' justification is no longer governing law. Do not classify all accountant-malpractice settlements as excluded.
entries.sourceRole: Week 3 assigned judicial opinion (reproduced in textbook)

entries.title: Recovery of loss
entries.summary: Receipt that restores a prior economic loss rather than adding new net wealth, potentially raising tax-benefit and basis questions.
entries.details: The text compares Clark's tax overpayment to an asset having recoverable basis; treatment may depend on whether an earlier deduction was taken.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 75
entries.laymanExplanation: If you lose $100 and later get that same $100 back, you may simply be recovering what you lost rather than making a new profit. The exact tax result depends on earlier deductions and the type of loss.
entries.legalExplanation: When a payment restores a prior loss, analyze whether it is genuinely replacing lost capital or taxable earnings, whether an original basis existed, and whether a past deduction yielded a tax benefit. Clark applies narrowly to an unnecessary tax payment caused by erroneous tax-filing advice.

entries.title: Tax benefit doctrine (preview)
entries.summary: A later recovery may be included in income to the extent an earlier deduction reduced tax.
entries.details: Introduced through the lost-pay-envelope hypothetical and addressed in more detail in a later chapter.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 77
entries.laymanExplanation: If a loss reduced your taxes last year and you later get that money back, the recovery may have to be included in income to undo the earlier tax advantage.
entries.legalExplanation: The tax benefit doctrine generally requires attention to whether an earlier deduction reduced tax and whether recovery in a later year is inconsistent with the circumstances supporting that deduction. The p.77 lost-envelope hypothetical is a preview; full doctrinal development appears later in the course.

entries.title: Clark fairness paradox
entries.summary: One reimbursed overpayer is better off than an uncompensated overpayer, but merely equal to a taxpayer who never overpaid.
entries.details: The text uses this to illustrate how tax rules define the relevant transaction and may leave some economic inequities.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 76
entries.legalExplanation: Clark's note compares an overpayer who received compensation (Akira), a similarly situated unreimbursed overpayer (Benito), and a taxpayer who was correctly advised (Cora). Whether the recovery is excluded depends on the choice of baseline. This is normative analysis, not a simple mechanical statutory rule.
entries.laymanExplanation: If an accountant repays someone who overpaid taxes, that person is now better off than someone whose accountant never repays them—but only as well off as someone whose taxes were done correctly in the first place.

entries.title: Actual tax liability versus tax overpayment
entries.summary: An actual tax liability is tax legally owed on the transactions undertaken; an overpayment is tax paid beyond that liability. Do not equate a potentially better tax strategy with an overpayment.
entries.details: In the government's 2018 McKenney brief, the McKenneys agreed with the IRS in a closing agreement that they owed approximately $2.2 million additional taxes for 2000–2005. They later obtained an $800,000 settlement from their accounting firm. The government argued that this recovered part of taxes actually owed, not tax they had overpaid through erroneous return preparation. The brief distinguishes an actual historical transaction from hypothetical, more favorable tax planning; these are the government's arguments, not the court's decision.
entries.examApplication: Compare Clark: Did the accountant cause payment beyond the taxpayer's actual legally correct tax, or did the taxpayer pay tax actually owed on the chosen transaction and later receive money from the accountant?
entries.examTrap: Tax that could have been avoided through a different transaction is not automatically an overpayment of tax actually owed. Keep the party's argument separate from a judicial holding.
entries.source: Assigned 'McKenny brief handout (1).pdf', five pages: government's redacted opening brief, Eleventh Circuit No. 18-10810, filed Sept. 6, 2018 (original appellate-brief pp. 21–24). This is government advocacy, not a judicial opinion.
entries.sourceRole: Definition and exam distinction derived from the government's assigned brief, not an attributed court holding.
entries.laymanExplanation: There is a difference between paying too much tax by mistake and paying the correct tax on a deal that turned out to be a bad tax-saving idea.
entries.sourceWeek: Week 3 — separately assigned McKenney government brief

entries.title: Old Colony principle — third-party payment of a taxpayer's tax
entries.summary: When another party pays a taxpayer's legally owed federal income tax on the taxpayer's behalf as a benefit, the discharge of that liability can constitute taxable income.
entries.details: The government's McKenney brief invoked Old Colony Trust Co. v. Commissioner, 279 U.S. 716 (1929), to argue that an accountant's settlement effectively reimbursing valid tax obligations should be included under §61. The handout does not reproduce the Old Colony judicial opinion, so Old Colony remains supporting cited authority, not a dedicated case brief. Whether a particular damages recovery is taxable also requires analysis of what the payment replaces.
entries.examApplication: Identify the underlying taxpayer liability and what a third-party payment actually reimburses. Contrast legal discharge or reimbursement of taxes owed with replacement of an amount paid unnecessarily because of a negligent filing choice.
entries.examTrap: Do not apply Old Colony automatically to all malpractice recoveries; Clark's actual-overpayment facts and the nature of the claimed loss may matter.
entries.source: Assigned 'McKenny brief handout (1).pdf', five pages: government's redacted opening brief, Eleventh Circuit No. 18-10810, filed Sept. 6, 2018 (original appellate-brief pp. 21–24). This is government advocacy, not a judicial opinion.
entries.sourceRole: Legal principle cited in the government's assigned brief; the case opinion is not reproduced in the handout.
entries.laymanExplanation: If your employer or another person pays a tax bill you actually owe for you, that can be the same as receiving money to pay it yourself.
entries.sourceWeek: Week 3 — separately assigned McKenney government brief

entries.title: Assigned supplemental advocacy — United States' brief in McKenney
entries.summary: The government argued an $800,000 accountant-malpractice settlement was taxable because it reimbursed valid tax liabilities, unlike the excess tax payment in Clark.
entries.details:
DOCUMENT TYPE: Government's redacted opening appellate brief filed September 6, 2018, not a judicial opinion.

FACTS AS ARGUED: Joseph and Amy McKenney used S corporations owned by an ESOP to structure consulting and dealership income. After examination, they signed a closing agreement accepting an IRS determination concerning an abusive ESOP transaction and acknowledged approximately $2.2 million in additional taxes for 2000–2005. They later settled malpractice claims against Grant Thornton for $800,000.

GOVERNMENT'S POSITION: The $800,000 replaced part of tax liabilities the taxpayers actually owed, and thus was income under §61 and Old Colony Trust. It distinguished Clark because Clark involved an accountant reimbursing tax actually overpaid. It also argued that tax consequences should follow transactions actually entered, not hypothetical restructuring that would have saved tax.

LIMITATION: These are arguments made by one litigant. The excerpt does not contain judicial findings or a court's holding. A 2020 court decision is separately linked in the current-law notes.
entries.examApplication: Exam comparison: Clark taxpayer overpaid due to erroneous filing advice; McKenney taxpayers' accountant advised transaction design and the government treated the additional tax on that actual transaction as legally owed. Explain why that difference matters for characterizing the settlement, while keeping the source's advocacy status clear.
entries.examTrap: Never cite the 2018 brief itself as the Eleventh Circuit's holding. The brief includes one party's characterization of the facts and the law.

entries.title: Recovery of capital versus return on capital
entries.summary: Getting original investment back is generally not income; earnings or proceeds beyond recoverable basis may be income.
entries.laymanExplanation: Lending someone $500 and being repaid $500 isn't a $500 profit. Extra interest is a separate gain.
entries.legalExplanation: The general recovery-of-capital principle distinguishes return of one's tax investment from income earned on it. Under gain computations, amount realized is reduced by allocated/adjusted basis, with separate treatment for dividends, rents, interest and other returns.
entries.details: The general recovery-of-capital principle distinguishes return of one's tax investment from income earned on it. Under gain computations, amount realized is reduced by allocated/adjusted basis, with separate treatment for dividends, rents, interest and other returns.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, textbook pp. 68–69; Week 3 syllabus-assigned.

topics.title: E. Personal & Business Injury Recoveries
topics.description: Character of damages, §104(a)(2), deferred settlements and constitutional questions.

entries.title: Business lost-profit damages are income
entries.summary: Amounts recovered to replace profits that would have been taxable are generally included in income.
entries.details: Settlement or insurance proceeds can be analyzed by what they replace; punitive damages also generally fall within §61.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 78
entries.laymanExplanation: If a business gets money to replace profits it missed out on, the payment is generally treated much like the profits would have been.
entries.legalExplanation: Damages replacing taxable business profits are generally income just as the underlying lost earnings would have been. The reading treats the recovery when received as income and distinguishes it from compensation for destruction of an asset with recoverable basis.

entries.title: Damages for destroyed business property — basis recovery
entries.summary: Recovery for damaged or destroyed property generally produces gain to the extent proceeds exceed adjusted basis; §1033 may permit qualifying deferral.
entries.details: Example from reading: $700,000 recovery for a building with $600,000 basis results in $100,000 gain absent qualifying nonrecognition.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 78
entries.laymanExplanation: If a destroyed building had $600,000 of tax basis and you receive $700,000 for it, the extra $100,000 can be gain, unless another rule postpones recognizing it.
entries.legalExplanation: Damages for damaged or destroyed business property can be a capital recovery; measure any gain by amount recovered minus applicable adjusted basis. The source's building example: $700,000 received for an asset with $600,000 basis creates potential $100,000 realized gain, before testing §1033 deferral.

entries.title: IRC §1033 — Involuntary conversions
entries.summary: Qualifying proceeds from destroyed or condemned business/investment property may receive nonrecognition when reinvested in eligible replacement property under statutory conditions.
entries.details: The reading uses it for compensation for a destroyed building; examine detailed replacement requirements in statutory text.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 78
entries.laymanExplanation: When qualifying property is destroyed or taken and you use the proceeds to buy suitable replacement property, tax law may let you delay reporting the gain.
entries.legalExplanation: Section 1033 provides nonrecognition rules for certain involuntary conversions of business/investment property into money when statutorily qualifying replacement property is obtained within the relevant time and conditions. The text illustrates replacement of a destroyed building; do not assume merely receiving insurance is automatically exempt.

entries.title: IRC §104(a)(2) — Physical injury or sickness damages
entries.summary: Qualifying damages (other than punitive damages) received on account of personal physical injuries or physical sickness are excluded from gross income.
entries.details: Applies to qualifying damages whether recovered by suit or agreement and in lump-sum or periodic form; the causal link to physical injury/sickness is critical.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 79
entries.examTrap: Nonphysical injury, reputational harm, or ordinary emotional distress does not by itself satisfy §104(a)(2). Punitive damages remain taxable.
entries.laymanExplanation: Money received as damages because of a physical injury or physical sickness can be tax-free, but punitive damages and many purely emotional-distress awards are different.
entries.legalExplanation: Section 104(a)(2) excludes qualifying damages received on account of personal physical injuries or physical sickness, other than punitive damages. The 1996 change restricted the exclusion and raised the question of nonphysical distress. Murphy II and Perez teach that the causal nature and legal source of payment matter more than whether a person suffered distress or pain.

entries.title: Compensatory versus punitive damages
entries.summary: Compensatory damages replace an identified loss; punitive damages are imposed as punishment or deterrence.
entries.details: For tax consequences examine the origin and purpose of payment, any statutory exclusion, and whether a return of capital is involved.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 79
entries.laymanExplanation: Compensatory damages aim to repay a loss. Punitive damages are an additional amount meant to punish the wrongdoer.
entries.legalExplanation: Compensatory damages restore or substitute for a specified loss, such as lost profits or personal injury; punitive damages add punishment/deterrence beyond compensation. Taxation depends on what is replaced and statutory exclusions; Glenshaw Glass includes punitive amounts absent exclusion, and §104(a)(2) expressly carves punitive amounts out.

entries.title: Origin of the claim
entries.summary: The factual and legal nature of the underlying claim that gives rise to damages.
entries.details: Distinguish recoveries for lost profits, destroyed property, physical personal injury, and reputation/emotional harms.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 79
entries.laymanExplanation: To classify lawsuit money for tax purposes, ask: 'What was this payment really for?' Lost wages, damaged property, and physical injury can have different tax outcomes.
entries.legalExplanation: The 'origin of the claim' looks at the actual right, injury or event for which damages were paid to classify tax consequences. A payment replacing wages or business profits, property value, physical pain and suffering, and reputational damage can be governed by different inclusion and basis rules.

entries.title: Murphy v. United States (Murphy II)
entries.summary: The D.C. Circuit held the award did not fall within §104(a)(2)'s physical-injury exclusion, was included in §61 gross income, and could constitutionally be taxed; the judgment was affirmed.
entries.details: The supplied text reproduces a judicial opinion, so this is a dedicated case brief.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), reproduced judicial opinion, Chapter 2 pp. 80–88.
entries.facts: Marrita Murphy recovered damages through an administrative whistleblower case against a former employer, including awards for emotional distress and reputational injury. She sought a refund of the income tax paid on those nonphysical-injury damages. On rehearing, the D.C. Circuit considered both the statute and Congress's taxing power.
entries.issue: Does §104(a)(2) exclude damages for emotional distress or reputational harm without a qualifying physical injury? If not, does §61 include those damages and may Congress constitutionally tax them?
entries.holding: On rehearing, the D.C. Circuit held the nonphysical-injury recovery was not excluded by §104(a)(2), fell within gross income under §61, and was constitutionally taxable; the taxpayer's challenge failed.
entries.reasoning: The 1996 amendment ties the §104(a)(2) exclusion to physical injury or physical sickness, and reputational/emotional harm alone does not qualify. The court read §61 broadly and reasoned the tax on the award was an excise on receipt/transaction rather than an unapportioned direct tax on property ownership. The prior Murphy I decision was vacated.
entries.rule: Nonphysical personal-injury damages are generally included under §61 absent another exclusion; §104(a)(2) is limited to qualifying physical injury/sickness damages (other than punitive), and Murphy II sustained taxation of its award as an excise.
entries.exam: Separate statutory analysis (§104, §61) from constitutional analysis (direct tax/apportionment). Do not substitute historical Murphy I for the rehearing holding.
entries.examApplication: Separate statutory analysis (§104, §61) from constitutional analysis (direct tax/apportionment). Do not substitute historical Murphy I for the rehearing holding.
entries.laymanExplanation: A whistleblower received damages for emotional harm and damage to reputation, not physical injury. The appeals court ruled the money was taxable and that Congress could tax it.
entries.examTrap: Emotional distress is not automatically a qualifying 'physical injury' solely because it causes bodily symptoms; analyze the precise statutory/regulatory conditions.
entries.sourceRole: Week 3 assigned judicial opinion (reproduced in textbook)

entries.title: Direct tax and apportionment
entries.summary: The Constitution requires certain direct federal taxes to be apportioned by population among states, subject to the Sixteenth Amendment for income taxes.
entries.details: Murphy II discusses Article I and distinguishes taxes on property ownership from taxes on transactions or activities.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 85
entries.laymanExplanation: For some taxes, the Constitution requires each state's tax share to follow its population. Federal income taxes have an important constitutional exception.
entries.legalExplanation: Article I requires certain direct taxes to be apportioned among states by population, while the Sixteenth Amendment removes apportionment for taxes on incomes. Murphy II distinguished a direct tax on owned property from an excise on a transaction or activity and sustained the tax on its damages award.

entries.title: Article I taxing power and constitutional limits
entries.summary: Congress has broad Article I power to lay taxes; direct taxes require apportionment except to the extent the Sixteenth Amendment permits unapportioned income taxes.
entries.details: The reproduced Murphy II excerpt reasons that taxing its award can be an excise on a transaction, satisfying the constitutional framework.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 85
entries.laymanExplanation: Congress has broad power to tax, but constitutional limits can affect particular taxes. The classification of the tax matters.
entries.legalExplanation: Congress has broad powers under Article I to impose income, excise and other taxes, subject to constitutional limitations. Murphy II reasoned the specific tax on receipt of nonphysical-injury damages was a constitutionally permissible excise, even when the taxpayer argued the amount was not income within the Sixteenth Amendment's meaning.

entries.title: Perez v. Commissioner
entries.summary: No. The payments were taxable compensation, not excludable damages for personal physical injury.
entries.details: The supplied text reproduces a judicial opinion, so this is a dedicated case brief.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), reproduced judicial opinion, Chapter 2 pp. 89–94.
entries.facts: Perez agreed with a fertility clinic to undergo hormone injections, medical monitoring, and multiple egg retrieval procedures to supply her eggs for others. She received $20,000 under written arrangements for undergoing the process, which involved pain, risk and physical intervention.
entries.issue: Were contractual payments for willingly undergoing egg-donation retrieval processes excludable 'damages' received on account of physical injury under §104(a)(2)?
entries.holding: No. The Tax Court held the $20,000 was taxable compensation, not qualifying personal physical-injury damages.
entries.reasoning: Perez voluntarily agreed to medical procedures in return for payment. Although they caused physical pain and risk, the clinic did not compensate a wrongful injury through damages; it paid consideration for contractually agreed actions. The post-1996 regulation's removal of a 'tort or tort-type' formal claim requirement did not make all compensation for painful activities damages.
entries.rule: Contract payments for voluntary services or procedures do not become §104(a)(2) injury damages merely because the services are physically invasive or painful.
entries.exam: Distinguish a settlement for a compensable physical injury from contractual pay for willingly performing a physically difficult activity.
entries.examApplication: Distinguish a settlement for a compensable physical injury from contractual pay for willingly performing a physically difficult activity.
entries.laymanExplanation: A woman was paid to go through an egg-retrieval process. The court said this was payment under a voluntary contract, not tax-free injury damages.
entries.examTrap: Pain alone does not show damages; identify the legal source and character of the payment.
entries.sourceRole: Week 3 assigned judicial opinion (reproduced in textbook)

entries.title: Structured settlement
entries.summary: A legal settlement that pays qualified damages over time rather than as a single lump sum.
entries.details: The textbook explains that qualifying periodic payments for physical injuries may receive special tax treatment, creating a timing advantage.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 94
entries.laymanExplanation: A structured settlement pays lawsuit compensation over time instead of in a single check.
entries.legalExplanation: A structured settlement spreads payments for an injury claim across time, often funded through an annuity or obligation of an assignee. The timing and character of the recovery, and the claimant's rights to immediate cash, affect tax analysis. The book focuses on qualifying physical-injury payments under §104(a)(2).

entries.title: Periodic payments for personal physical injury
entries.summary: Under §104(a)(2), qualifying physical-injury damages may be excludable whether paid in a lump sum or periodic payments.
entries.details: Structured settlements require careful analysis of entitlement and economic control; the reading highlights favorable treatment of certain deferred-payment components.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 94
entries.laymanExplanation: Qualifying physical-injury compensation may remain excluded even when paid in installments, subject to the applicable rules.
entries.legalExplanation: A qualifying personal physical-injury recovery can be excludable under §104(a)(2) whether received all at once or in periodic payments, assuming the statutory conditions are satisfied. The source contrasts immediate lump-sum funds invested by the claimant with fixed structured payments administered through a settlement vehicle.

entries.title: Policy rationale for physical injury exclusion
entries.summary: Compensation arguably restores lost physical well-being rather than creating a net economic gain.
entries.details: The text contrasts physical with emotional/reputational injuries and asks why nominally similar compensation can be taxed differently.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 79
entries.legalExplanation: The book contrasts compensatory recovery for physical injury with nonphysical harm. If an award restores a person's situation after an accident, an exclusion might seem fair, but comparison against someone equally injured without an award can suggest the opposite. This is policy rationale, not a substitute for §104's text.
entries.laymanExplanation: Should injury compensation be tax-free because it only repairs what you lost? The book compares someone who is paid damages with someone who suffers the same injury but gets nothing.

entries.title: IRC §104(a)(2) — distinguish physical and nonphysical injury awards
entries.summary: Qualifying physical-injury damages may be excluded; damages for purely nonphysical harm generally do not qualify under §104(a)(2).
entries.laymanExplanation: Money for a broken leg may qualify for a tax exclusion. Money for damage to your reputation usually doesn't qualify simply because it was emotionally painful.
entries.legalExplanation: The 1996 amendment limits §104(a)(2) to damages received on account of personal physical injuries or physical sickness (other than punitive damages). The award's purpose and causation matter. The reading's Murphy II and Perez opinions emphasize statutory text and the nature of the claim.
entries.details: The 1996 amendment limits §104(a)(2) to damages received on account of personal physical injuries or physical sickness (other than punitive damages). The award's purpose and causation matter. The reading's Murphy II and Perez opinions emphasize statutory text and the nature of the claim.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, textbook pp. 78–94; Week 3 syllabus-assigned.
entries.examTrap: The word 'injury' by itself isn't enough; determine whether the source of the payment is a qualifying physical injury or sickness.

entries.title: Damages received on account of injury
entries.summary: For §104, whether damages were received 'on account of' a qualifying injury is a causal question, not merely a label on a settlement.
entries.laymanExplanation: Ask what the check is actually paying for. Is it compensation because the person was physically injured, or payment for something else?
entries.legalExplanation: The text analyzes compensation for lost business profits, harm to property, physical personal injury, emotional distress, reputational harm and voluntary contractual bodily services. Their tax treatments differ because the origin and reason for payment differ.
entries.details: The text analyzes compensation for lost business profits, harm to property, physical personal injury, emotional distress, reputational harm and voluntary contractual bodily services. Their tax treatments differ because the origin and reason for payment differ.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, textbook pp. 79–94; Week 3 syllabus-assigned.

entries.title: Qualified structured settlement / periodic payments
entries.summary: A qualifying personal physical-injury settlement may pay amounts over time, with §104(a)(2) addressing qualifying periodic awards.
entries.laymanExplanation: Instead of one check today, an injured person might get monthly payments for years. The tax outcome depends on the nature of the damages and how the deal is structured.
entries.legalExplanation: The reading describes structured settlements as periodic damage payments with favorable treatment under §104(a)(2) for qualifying physical injury or sickness. Contractual control, the purchaser or assignee's role, and payment design can affect tax consequences. Distinguish this from taxable investment income earned after an unrestricted lump-sum payment.
entries.details: The reading describes structured settlements as periodic damage payments with favorable treatment under §104(a)(2) for qualifying physical injury or sickness. Contractual control, the purchaser or assignee's role, and payment design can affect tax consequences. Distinguish this from taxable investment income earned after an unrestricted lump-sum payment.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, textbook pp. 94–95; Week 3 syllabus-assigned.

topics.title: F. Illegal Income
topics.description: Taxability of unlawful gains, claims of right and restitution.

entries.title: Illegal proceeds may be taxable gross income
entries.summary: Unlawful gains can constitute gross income under §61, even if the recipient may later be required to repay them.
entries.details: James v. United States is referenced for the general principle: receipt without consensual recognition of an obligation to repay and without restriction can be taxable.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 96
entries.examTrap: Illegal character of income does not remove it from §61.
entries.laymanExplanation: You don't get an income-tax exemption because the money came from something illegal. Stolen or embezzled money can be taxable.
entries.legalExplanation: Illegal gain is not outside §61 solely because obtaining it was unlawful. James v. United States is cited for treating embezzlement proceeds as income when the recipient acquires funds without consensual repayment obligation or meaningful restrictions. The later possibility of restitution does not itself erase current inclusion.

entries.title: Claim of right
entries.summary: A taxpayer's practical dominion over funds, without an acknowledged limitation or consensual obligation to repay, may support current inclusion.
entries.details: The source compares typical embezzlement proceeds against loans or prompt secured repayment arrangements.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 97
entries.laymanExplanation: If you receive money and can use it as your own without accepting a genuine duty to return it, tax law may treat you as having income right now.
entries.legalExplanation: Under the claim-of-right principle, receipt of money under a claim of free use and without consensual acknowledgment of a repayment obligation may count as current income even when the taxpayer might later have to restore it. Compare genuine borrowing with theft or embezzlement.

entries.title: Obligation to repay
entries.summary: A recognized duty to return money, relevant to whether receipt is a taxable accession to wealth or nonincome borrowing.
entries.details: Do not mistake a purely subjective intention to repay for a legally and factually supported borrowing obligation.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 97
entries.laymanExplanation: Borrowing money usually isn't income because you have a real obligation to pay it back. An empty promise to repay may not be enough.
entries.legalExplanation: A loan principal normally does not enrich the borrower because a genuine corresponding liability to repay arises. Gilbert's exceptional result turned on immediate secured obligations, reasonable expectation of repayment, contemporaneous notice and restrictions on use; an after-the-fact promise does not settle taxability.

entries.title: Gilbert v. Commissioner
entries.summary: The Second Circuit reversed the Tax Court; under its unusual facts, the withdrawals were not income when acquired.
entries.details: The supplied text reproduces a judicial opinion, so this is a dedicated case brief.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), reproduced judicial opinion, Chapter 2 pp. 95–99.
entries.facts: Gilbert, president of Bruce corporation, caused unauthorized withdrawals totaling $1,958,000 for stock margin calls, repaid $5,000 and executed notes for $1,953,000. He promptly disclosed the withdrawals to certain officers and counsel and gave Bruce security over assets then worth more than the money owed. The board accepted the collateral but refused to ratify the withdrawals; later repayment efforts collapsed.
entries.issue: Did these unauthorized corporate withdrawals constitute taxable embezzlement income under James despite a recognized repayment duty and prompt overcollateralization?
entries.holding: The Second Circuit reversed the Tax Court. On these unusual facts, Gilbert did not realize taxable income when he withdrew the funds because they functioned as a genuinely secured obligation to repay.
entries.reasoning: Gilbert intended to return the funds, believed corporate approval would follow, promptly informed officers and counsel, issued demand notes, and subjected assets exceeding the liability to creditor control. The court distinguished typical embezzlement, where there is no contemporaneous consensual recognition of repayment obligation or restrictions on use.
entries.rule: James does not automatically make every unauthorized withdrawal income; a narrow exception may apply where genuine contemporaneous repayment obligation, reasonable expectation of repayment, anticipated consent and prompt adequate security are shown.
entries.exam: Compare a conventional unsecured theft/embezzlement with Gilbert's immediate secured loan-like transaction; identify consent, intent, collateral, timing and actual freedom to use funds.
entries.examApplication: Compare a conventional unsecured theft/embezzlement with Gilbert's immediate secured loan-like transaction; identify consent, intent, collateral, timing and actual freedom to use funds.
entries.laymanExplanation: A company executive took money without permission but promptly gave real security and acknowledged repayment. The court treated those unusual facts differently from ordinary embezzlement.
entries.examTrap: A belated note or subjective promise to repay stolen money is not enough to create Gilbert's exceptional result.
entries.sourceRole: Week 3 assigned judicial opinion (reproduced in textbook)

entries.title: James v. United States (supporting citation)
entries.summary: The textbook cites James for the general taxability of embezzled funds.
entries.details: James is referenced within Gilbert; it is not a separately reproduced assigned opinion in the supplied pages.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 97
entries.legalExplanation: James v. United States is mentioned in Gilbert for the rule that embezzled money can constitute income. Wilcox, earlier excluding such receipts because of a duty to restore them, was overruled by James; the chapter's reference cases should remain supporting citations, not dedicated opinion briefs.
entries.laymanExplanation: The law generally taxes money stolen or embezzled, even if the thief has to repay it later. This cited Supreme Court case helps explain that point.

entries.title: James and Wilcox — supporting historical authorities
entries.summary: The textbook explains that James v. United States overruled Wilcox's prior exclusion of embezzlement receipts; they are citations in the Gilbert notes, not reproduced opinions.
entries.laymanExplanation: Stolen money can count as taxable income. Older Supreme Court decisions disagreed, but the later rule generally includes embezzled proceeds.
entries.legalExplanation: The book notes that James v. United States, 366 U.S. 213 (1961), displaced Commissioner v. Wilcox, 327 U.S. 404 (1946), which had excluded embezzled money based on an obligation to restore it. Gilbert distinguishes certain secured withdrawals from typical embezzlement. No extra case briefs should be generated for James or Wilcox.
entries.details: The book notes that James v. United States, 366 U.S. 213 (1961), displaced Commissioner v. Wilcox, 327 U.S. 404 (1946), which had excluded embezzled money based on an obligation to restore it. Gilbert distinguishes certain secured withdrawals from typical embezzlement. No extra case briefs should be generated for James or Wilcox.

topics.title: G. Gain on Sale of a Home
topics.description: Section 121 home-sale gain exclusion and limitations.

entries.title: IRC §121 — Principal residence exclusion
entries.summary: A qualifying taxpayer may exclude up to $250,000 of gain on sale of a principal residence, or generally $500,000 for qualifying joint filers.
entries.details: General rule: taxpayer owned and used the property as principal residence for at least two years during the five-year period ending at sale; subject to frequency, filing and other conditions.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 100
entries.elements: Ownership and principal residence use: generally 2 of the 5 years before sale. Standard cap: $250,000; qualifying MFJ cap: $500,000.
entries.examTrap: A vacation property does not qualify merely because it is owned for two years; the principal-residence use requirement matters.
entries.laymanExplanation: When you sell your main home, the law may let you leave a large portion of the profit out of income tax if you meet ownership and living-in-the-home requirements.
entries.legalExplanation: Section 121(a) generally requires both ownership and use of a home as a principal residence for periods totaling at least 2 years during the 5 years before sale. The ordinary gain exclusion is capped at $250,000 for qualifying individual filers. Analyze whether the use and ownership tests were met and whether other special rules apply.

entries.title: IRC §121 — Joint-return conditions
entries.summary: A $500,000 exclusion for qualifying married joint filers generally requires meeting joint-return, use, ownership and other statutory requirements.
entries.details: The reading notes that both spouses must satisfy the use test, while the ownership condition can be satisfied under the statutory joint-filer rules.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 101
entries.laymanExplanation: A married couple filing jointly may qualify for a higher home-sale exclusion, but they must satisfy extra conditions.
entries.legalExplanation: Section 121(b)(2) allows up to $500,000 exclusion for qualifying married joint filers, generally requiring that either spouse meet ownership conditions and both meet use requirements plus other conditions. The source separately mentions surviving-spouse treatment under §121(b)(4).

entries.title: IRC §121 — Once-every-two-years limit
entries.summary: A taxpayer generally cannot claim the full §121 exclusion if it was used on a different sale within the preceding two years.
entries.details: The reading discusses reduced exclusions when sales arise from qualifying changes in employment, health, or certain unforeseen circumstances.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 101
entries.laymanExplanation: You generally cannot use the full main-home sale exclusion every year. The law usually requires a two-year gap, with some exceptions.
entries.legalExplanation: Section 121 generally prevents an eligible taxpayer from using the full exclusion for another residence sale within the preceding 2 years. Section 121(c) can allow a reduced exclusion for certain moves involving work, health or unforeseen circumstances. Calculate the appropriate tax-year cap and exceptions.

entries.title: Principal residence
entries.summary: The home that serves as the taxpayer's main residence for purposes of §121's use requirement.
entries.details: This characterization is factual and distinct from owning a secondary home or investment property.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 100
entries.laymanExplanation: Your principal residence is the place that actually functions as your main home, not just any house you own.
entries.legalExplanation: Principal residence means the property used as the taxpayer's main home, not merely any owned property, for purposes of §121. Facts about actual residence and occupancy matter, and vacation or investment properties do not qualify just because they appreciate.

entries.title: Taxable gain after §121 exclusion
entries.summary: Taxable gain = max(0, realized home-sale gain − allowable §121 exclusion).
entries.details: Textbook example: single taxpayer's $100,000-basis residence sold for $400,000; realized gain $300,000, $250,000 excluded, $50,000 taxable (assuming full eligibility).
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 101
entries.examApplication: Compute realized gain first, then determine §121 eligibility and exclusion limit.
entries.laymanExplanation: First calculate profit from selling your home. Then subtract the part the law lets you exclude. The remaining amount may be taxable.
entries.legalExplanation: For an eligible principal-residence sale, first calculate realized gain as amount realized less adjusted basis, then subtract the exclusion allowed under §121, keeping taxable gain no lower than zero. Book example: sale $400,000, basis $100,000 → $300,000 realized gain; single-filer $250,000 exclusion → $50,000 taxable.

entries.title: Pre-1997 home-sale gain rules
entries.summary: Former §1034 allowed rollover-style gain deferral on reinvestment in another home; prior §121 had a one-time older-taxpayer exclusion.
entries.details: These rules are repealed and appear in the reading only to explain the current §121 regime.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Chapter 2, p. 102

legalWarning.label: REPEALED PRE-1997 LAW
legalWarning.reason: The old §1034 rollover provision and previous one-time home-sale exclusion were superseded by the 1997 enactment of current §121.

entries.legalExplanation: Before 1997, a repealed §1034 rollover rule and older one-time §121 exclusion treated qualifying home sales differently. The current regime derives from Congress's 1997 redesign; these are purely historical notes, not controlling exam computations.
entries.laymanExplanation: There used to be different rules for selling your house. The old system was repealed and replaced in 1997, so it is background rather than an exam rule today.

entries.title: IRC §121(c) — reduced exclusion for qualifying early home sales
entries.summary: When a taxpayer fails the ordinary ownership/use or frequency rules, a reduced maximum exclusion may apply for qualifying employment, health or unforeseen-circumstance reasons.
entries.laymanExplanation: If you must move for a new job after living in your home only one year, you might still exclude part of the profit rather than losing the entire break.
entries.legalExplanation: The reading illustrates a single taxpayer transferred to a new office after one year who may qualify for a proportional $125,000 ceiling instead of the full $250,000. §121(c) requires identifying the qualifying reason and determining a statutory reduced amount; do not assume every early sale qualifies.

entries.title: IRC §121(b)(4) — qualifying surviving spouse
entries.summary: A surviving spouse may qualify for the $500,000 home-sale gain limit for a sale within two years of the other spouse's death, if statutory requirements are met.
entries.laymanExplanation: If someone's spouse dies, they may still have a limited period to use the higher married-couple home-sale exclusion when selling the house.
entries.legalExplanation: The source notes §121(b)(4), which permits a qualifying surviving spouse to receive a $500,000 limit for a sale within two years after the spouse's death when requisite ownership/use and other conditions are met.
entries.details: The source notes §121(b)(4), which permits a qualifying surviving spouse to receive a $500,000 limit for a sale within two years after the spouse's death when requisite ownership/use and other conditions are met.
