entries.title: Imputed income
entries.summary: Nonmarket value derived from one's own work or use of one's own property is generally not taxable.
entries.laymanExplanation: Fixing your own car saves you money, but you do not report imagined mechanic wages.
entries.legalExplanation: The source distinguishes imputed income from market exchange. The primary categories are self-provided household labor and the rental value of living in owner-occupied housing. This economic benefit ordinarily is not included under §61.
entries.details: The source distinguishes imputed income from market exchange. The primary categories are self-provided household labor and the rental value of living in owner-occupied housing. This economic benefit ordinarily is not included under §61.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., Week 3 assigned pp. 112–114

entries.title: Psychic income
entries.summary: Subjective happiness or pleasure is not measured as taxable income.
entries.laymanExplanation: Enjoying a sunset or an extra vacation week does not create a separate tax charge.
entries.legalExplanation: Psychic income reflects subjective satisfaction or enjoyment, unlike market-measurable consumption. The source explains that taxing leisure would be intrusive and administratively impracticable.
entries.details: Psychic income reflects subjective satisfaction or enjoyment, unlike market-measurable consumption. The source explains that taxing leisure would be intrusive and administratively impracticable.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., Week 3 assigned pp. 114–116

entries.title: In-kind income
entries.summary: Property or services received as market compensation generally constitute income, despite the absence of cash.
entries.laymanExplanation: A lawyer who gets house painting in exchange for legal work may have taxable income even though no money changes hands.
entries.legalExplanation: Gross income under §61 includes income realized in money, property, or services. Noncash employer benefits may be excluded under specific statutes such as §§119 and 132.
entries.details: Gross income under §61 includes income realized in money, property, or services. Noncash employer benefits may be excluded under specific statutes such as §§119 and 132.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., Week 3 assigned pp. 114–116

entries.title: Private sphere versus public sphere
entries.summary: Private transactions generally occur within the household; public transactions involve market exchanges with others.
entries.laymanExplanation: Babysitting your own child is different from providing childcare to a stranger in exchange for repairs.
entries.legalExplanation: The source distinguishes market-based labor and property exchanges from household and self-provision activity. Tax consequences can differ sharply even where the economic benefit is similar.
entries.details: The source distinguishes market-based labor and property exchanges from household and self-provision activity. Tax consequences can differ sharply even where the economic benefit is similar.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., Week 3 assigned pp. 111–112

entries.title: Imputed rental value of a home
entries.summary: An owner-occupant benefits by not paying rent to another landlord; that hypothetical rent is not ordinarily taxed.
entries.laymanExplanation: If you live in the house you own, the IRS does not normally charge you income tax on imagined rent to yourself.
entries.legalExplanation: The source compares investing $1 million in bonds and paying rent with buying a home to occupy. Bond interest is taxable; owner-occupied housing value is not included as imputed rent. This creates an asymmetric tax preference.
entries.details: The source compares investing $1 million in bonds and paying rent with buying a home to occupy. Bond interest is taxable; owner-occupied housing value is not included as imputed rent. This creates an asymmetric tax preference.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., Week 3 assigned pp. 113–114

entries.title: Barter and reciprocal services are generally included in gross income
entries.summary: When two people trade valuable services, each generally has income equal to the fair market value received.
entries.laymanExplanation: A babysitter trades $100 in childcare for $100 of painting; both may have $100 of income.
entries.legalExplanation: Under Reg. §1.61-2(d)(1), services paid for with property or other services are generally valued at FMV. Self-service without a negotiated market exchange is treated differently; personal consumption costs typically are not deductible.

entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., Week 3 assigned pp. 115–117

entries.title: Revenue Ruling 79-24 — reciprocal services and art-for-rent
entries.summary: Both sides of taxable barter transactions include the fair market value of services, property, or rental use received.
entries.laymanExplanation: A lawyer swaps legal work for painting; an artist exchanges artwork for apartment rent. Both sides receive taxable value.
entries.legalExplanation: The assigned revenue ruling applies §61 and Reg. §1.61-2(d)(1). Situation 1: legal and painting services are exchanged; each includes FMV received. Situation 2: the apartment owner includes FMV of art and the artist includes rental value. It is an IRS ruling, not a judicial opinion.
entries.details: The assigned revenue ruling applies §61 and Reg. §1.61-2(d)(1). Situation 1: legal and painting services are exchanged; each includes FMV received. Situation 2: the apartment owner includes FMV of art and the artist includes rental value. It is an IRS ruling, not a judicial opinion.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., Week 3 assigned pp. 116–117

entries.title: Barter exchange reporting — §6045
entries.summary: Organized barter exchanges may have information-reporting duties; casual swaps of similar services on a noncommercial basis receive separate treatment.
entries.laymanExplanation: A service-credit trade club may report its members' trades to the IRS; informal neighbors helping each other can be different.
entries.legalExplanation: The source cites §6045 and Reg. §1.6045-1(a)(4), which excludes arrangements solely for informal noncommercial exchange of similar services from the defined reporting barter exchange. Reporting and inclusion are separate questions.
entries.details: The source cites §6045 and Reg. §1.6045-1(a)(4), which excludes arrangements solely for informal noncommercial exchange of similar services from the defined reporting barter exchange. Reporting and inclusion are separate questions.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., Week 3 assigned pp. 117–118

entries.title: Implicit tax and tax capitalization
entries.summary: Tax-favored investments can command higher prices and lower pretax yields as investors compete for tax savings.
entries.laymanExplanation: You might accept a 6% tax-free municipal bond return instead of a 10% taxable bond return; the yield difference is the hidden cost of the break.
entries.legalExplanation: The source uses §103 municipal bonds to demonstrate implicit taxation and tax capitalization. A 10% taxable return versus 6% tax-free comparable return implies 40% reduced yield by this simplified comparison. This is not a tax payment to the Treasury.

entries.examApplication: Implicit tax = (10% − 6%)/10% = 40%; assume comparable risk, maturity and market pricing.

entries.title: Substitute taxation
entries.summary: Tax law may limit the payor's deductions rather than directly including a hard-to-value benefit in the recipient's income.
entries.laymanExplanation: Instead of tracking every free lunch an employee eats, the law might deny some of the employer's expense deduction.
entries.legalExplanation: The source uses consumer furniture assembly and employer-provided meals to illustrate compensating for untaxed private or fringe benefits by taxing an easier-to-observe side of the exchange. This is a policy design mechanism, not a generally applicable statutory inclusion test.

entries.title: Added leisure versus added compensation
entries.summary: Equal annual salaries generally produce equal reported wage income even when one worker receives more vacation days.
entries.laymanExplanation: Two workers earn $60,000, but one has an extra week off. The salary is the same for income-tax calculation.
entries.legalExplanation: Paid leisure changes effective hourly pay, but tax law generally does not separately impute a taxable dollar value for foregone possible work during additional vacation days.
entries.details: Paid leisure changes effective hourly pay, but tax law generally does not separately impute a taxable dollar value for foregone possible work during additional vacation days.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., Week 3 assigned pp. 115–116

entries.title: Why private benefits are ignored
entries.summary: Privacy, valuation, enforceability and behavioral consequences complicate taxing the private sphere.
entries.laymanExplanation: The government does not inspect your home repairs or measure your happiness, even though those can make you better off.
entries.legalExplanation: The book emphasizes stay-at-home labor, self-provision, owner-occupied housing, and tax preference effects. This is supplementary policy rather than an exam rule.

topics.title: B. Gifts — §102 and Commissioner v. Duberstein
topics.description: The textbook's Week 3 pp.119–134, plus separately assigned Harris opinion (pp.154–161) kept distinct.

entries.title: IRC §102(a) — recipient exclusion for genuine gifts and bequests
entries.summary: Property acquired by gift, bequest, devise or inheritance is generally excluded from the recipient's income.
entries.laymanExplanation: If your parent gives you a real present out of love, you normally do not pay income tax just for receiving it.
entries.legalExplanation: §102(a) excludes qualifying gifts and inheritances. However, §102 does not turn compensation into a gift merely by label. The casebook contrasts Donna giving Edward $30,000 as a gift (recipient excludes, donor no deduction) with wages for personal services. Gift-tax matters are separate.
entries.details: §102(a) excludes qualifying gifts and inheritances. However, §102 does not turn compensation into a gift merely by label. The casebook contrasts Donna giving Edward $30,000 as a gift (recipient excludes, donor no deduction) with wages for personal services. Gift-tax matters are separate.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Week 3 pp. 120–123
entries.examApplication: Donna earns $100,000, gives adult son Edward $30,000 out of affection. She has no ordinary personal deduction, and Edward excludes the gift.
entries.examTrap: A purported romantic-partner gift still requires donor motive under Duberstein and does not establish criminal tax willfulness under Harris.

entries.title: Detached and disinterested generosity / donor's motive
entries.summary: The giver's purpose is the central inquiry: generosity and affection favor gift status; expected business return or compensation weighs against.
entries.laymanExplanation: A Cadillac called a present may really be payment if it rewards someone for profitable customer leads.
entries.legalExplanation: Duberstein applies §102's colloquial gift concept to total factual circumstances. Detached/disinterested refers to absence of a commercial exchange, not the donor's indifference. No rigid test substitutes for determining the transferor's intention.
entries.details: Duberstein applies §102's colloquial gift concept to total factual circumstances. Detached/disinterested refers to absence of a commercial exchange, not the donor's indifference. No rigid test substitutes for determining the transferor's intention.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Week 3 pp. 123–130
entries.examApplication: Review transferor statements, relationship circumstances, requests for services, timing and contemporaneous documents. Contrast gift-classification under Duberstein with criminal willfulness under Harris.

entries.title: Duberstein — gift is a fact-sensitive classification
entries.summary: Gift status under §102 is determined from the overall facts and the transferor's motivation, not merely voluntariness, wording, or formal obligations.
entries.laymanExplanation: Someone can willingly hand you money and still be paying for a job you did.
entries.legalExplanation: A gift need not follow a legal obligation, but absence of legal duty is not conclusive. The donor's intended economic benefit, the recipient's services, contemporaneous correspondence, business deductibility, and surrounding relationships matter. Appellate review generally respects factual findings absent clear error.
entries.details: A gift need not follow a legal obligation, but absence of legal duty is not conclusive. The donor's intended economic benefit, the recipient's services, contemporaneous correspondence, business deductibility, and surrounding relationships matter. Appellate review generally respects factual findings absent clear error.

entries.title: IRC §102(c) — employer transfers to employees
entries.summary: An employer's transfer to or for the benefit of an employee generally cannot qualify for the §102(a) gift exclusion.
entries.laymanExplanation: A company generally cannot make your bonus tax-free just by saying it is a gift.
entries.legalExplanation: The 1986 statutory enactment of §102(c) generally overrode the historical Stanton outcome from the consolidated Duberstein case. Specific other exclusions, such as qualifying §74(c) achievement awards, may apply.
entries.details: The 1986 statutory enactment of §102(c) generally overrode the historical Stanton outcome from the consolidated Duberstein case. Specific other exclusions, such as qualifying §74(c) achievement awards, may apply.

legalWarning.label: STANTON RULE SUPERSEDED
legalWarning.reason: Congress added §102(c) in 1986 and generally disallowed employer-to-employee gift exclusion, unlike the historical outcome following remand.

entries.examTrap: Do not use Stanton's 1960-era treatment as present-day law for employer bonuses.

entries.title: Tips and service-related gratuities are taxable
entries.summary: Ordinary gratuities received for services are compensation under §61 and Reg. §1.61-2(a)(1).
entries.laymanExplanation: A waiter getting a tip has earned money even if a customer gives it voluntarily.
entries.legalExplanation: The casebook discusses restaurant tips, clergyman marriage fees and casino gaming gratuities. The referenced McCormick and Olk decisions appear only as citations; they are not independently reproduced opinions.

entries.title: IRC §74 — prizes and awards
entries.summary: Most prizes and awards are gross income unless a specific statutory exception is satisfied.
entries.laymanExplanation: Winning a car or cash in a contest is normally taxable.
entries.legalExplanation: §74 includes prizes and awards, with statutory exceptions for certain qualifying donated prizes, and eligible employee achievement awards under §74(c). The receiving taxpayer must establish the conditions for an applicable exception.

entries.title: IRC §117 — qualified scholarship amounts
entries.summary: Qualified scholarship funds for degree candidates used for tuition, mandatory fees and required educational materials can be excluded, but service compensation is generally taxable.
entries.laymanExplanation: A tuition scholarship may be tax-free; pay for teaching or research is usually taxable compensation.
entries.legalExplanation: §117's statutory scholarship exclusion is limited to specified educational costs for eligible degree candidates. Amounts received as consideration for services (subject to exceptions elsewhere in statute) are generally not excluded by §117.

entries.title: Bequests versus payment for prior services
entries.summary: A true inheritance is ordinarily excluded; testamentary property promised as consideration for services can be taxable income.
entries.laymanExplanation: If a lawyer works for free in exchange for a promise of money in a will, the later will payment can be taxable compensation.
entries.legalExplanation: The casebook contrasts Wolder (contractually promised bequest for services treated as income), McDonald (appreciation bequest excludable) and Lyeth (will contest proceeds deemed bequest). Those are supporting references only; no separate opinions reproduced in assigned pp111–134.

entries.title: General welfare exclusion
entries.summary: Some need-based welfare, disaster and victim-relief benefits are administratively treated as outside gross income.
entries.laymanExplanation: Certain government aid payments do not go on your income-tax return even though they give you cash or help.
entries.legalExplanation: The source contrasts general-welfare administrative treatment of qualifying relief with unemployment benefits now included under §85. TANF assistance with work requirements can raise characterization issues, and IRS Notice 99-3 states conditions under which TANF assistance remains welfare rather than wages.

TANF assistance with work requirements can raise characterization issues, and IRS Notice 99-3 states conditions under which TANF assistance remains welfare rather than wages.

entries.title: IRC §85 — unemployment compensation
entries.summary: Unemployment benefits are generally taxable income under §85 absent a specific tax-year exception.
entries.laymanExplanation: Unlike some welfare payments, unemployment checks normally go in taxable income.
entries.legalExplanation: The casebook notes an exceptional temporary 2020 COVID-era exclusion; current general treatment is inclusion under §85 rather than a §102 gift.
entries.details: The casebook notes an exceptional temporary 2020 COVID-era exclusion; current general treatment is inclusion under §85 rather than a §102 gift.

entries.title: IRC §86 — taxable portion of Social Security benefits
entries.summary: Depending on combined income, zero to 85% of Social Security benefits can be included in gross income.
entries.laymanExplanation: A person receiving Social Security may owe tax on part of those benefits, not on all of them in every case.
entries.legalExplanation: The casebook outlines a statutory combined-income analysis using AGI, tax-exempt interest and one-half of benefits, with joint-filer threshold amounts $32,000 and $44,000. The full piecewise formula is in §86, and the 85% figure is a maximum portion included, not the rate charged on those benefits.

The full piecewise formula is in §86, and the 85% figure is a maximum portion included, not the rate charged on those benefits.

entries.examTrap: 85% inclusion is NOT an 85% tax rate; the actual rate depends on taxable-income brackets.

entries.title: Donor versus donee income tax consequences
entries.summary: The donor's tax and deduction are separate from the donee's gift exclusion.
entries.laymanExplanation: When someone gives their adult child $30,000 as a true gift, neither a tax deduction for the parent nor income for the child automatically results.
entries.legalExplanation: In the source's Donna–Edward example, Donna still has $100,000 of earned income with no personal deduction for a $30,000 transfer, while Edward excludes the $30,000 under §102. This is distinct from transfer tax considerations.
entries.details: In the source's Donna–Edward example, Donna still has $100,000 of earned income with no personal deduction for a $30,000 transfer, while Edward excludes the $30,000 under §102. This is distinct from transfer tax considerations.

entries.examTrap: A recipient's income-tax exclusion does not resolve any separately applicable donor-side gift or estate tax.

entries.title: Business gift versus compensation
entries.summary: A business-motivated transfer can be a genuine gift, but payment intended to reward or induce services is normally income.
entries.laymanExplanation: A store might send a thank-you present, but paying someone for new customers is compensation even if it comes wrapped as a gift.
entries.legalExplanation: Under Duberstein, business purpose, deduction, and corporate identity are evidence but not automatic legal bars to §102. The notes discuss §274(b)'s $25 business-gift deduction cap as a separate, payor-side rule.

entries.title: Why the Code excludes gifts despite economic enrichment
entries.summary: Privacy, family unit treatment, and administrative burden motivate gift exclusions.
entries.laymanExplanation: Gifts make people richer, but checking every birthday gift would be intrusive and impractical.
entries.legalExplanation: The source contrasts Haig–Simons broad economic income with §102's statutory exclusion and debates alternatives that might tax the recipient, allow donor deduction, both or neither.

entries.title: Commissioner v. Duberstein (with Stanton v. United States)
entries.summary: The Supreme Court sustained the Tax Court's finding that Duberstein's Cadillac was business remuneration, and remanded Stanton for clearer factfinding.
entries.laymanExplanation: A businessman got a Cadillac after sending useful leads to another business. The Court said calling it a gift wasn't enough. Another payment called a 'gratuity' needed clearer factfinding.
entries.facts: Duberstein gave business acquaintance Berman information about possible customers. Berman insisted on gifting a Cadillac to thank him; the donor's company treated it as a business deduction. Duberstein said he never intended compensation. Separately, a church-related corporation awarded departing employee Stanton a $20,000 payment called a gratuity in appreciation of his years of service; the trial court made only a conclusory gift finding.
entries.issue: What makes a transfer a 'gift' excluded by §102(a), and how should appellate courts review trial-level findings about motive?
entries.holding: Duberstein: The Supreme Court reversed the Sixth Circuit and reinstated the Tax Court's permissible factual determination that the Cadillac was payment for business services, not a gift. Stanton: The Second Circuit judgment was vacated and the matter remanded for adequate findings; the Supreme Court did not hold categorically that his gratuity was a gift.
entries.reasoning: The statutory gift concept relies on the transferor's dominant purpose, not simply voluntariness or lack of duty. Detached/disinterested generosity suggests gift; remuneration or hoped-for economic benefit suggests income. Business deduction and corporate status matter but are not conclusive. The decision largely places the question with the factfinder, with limited appellate reversal for clear error.
entries.rule: For §102(a), examine the transferor's actual intention and whole factual record: affection or detached generosity versus anticipated business benefit or services. Neither labels nor voluntary payment decide by themselves.
entries.exam: Analyze donor intent, services, quid pro quo, reimbursement, business records, and the limits on appellate factual review. Apply §102(c) separately for post-1986 employer-to-employee transfers.
entries.examApplication: A supplier sends a car to a consultant who found customers for the supplier. Assess business motives despite references to a gift; if employment relationship exists, add §102(c).
entries.examTrap: The Court did not announce all corporate transfers are income or all personal transfers are gifts. Stanton's historical ultimate classification is limited by later §102(c).
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., reproduced Supreme Court opinion, assigned Week 3 printed pp.123–129.
entries.sourceRole: Opinion reproduced in syllabus-assigned textbook excerpt — dedicated case brief.

topics.assignmentSource: Week 3 syllabus: Chapter 3 pp111–134 + assigned Harris handout

entries.title: Harris — Gift versus paid services in a personal relationship
entries.summary: A gift reflects the transferor's donative motive; compensation is paid for services, duties, or anticipated economic return.
entries.details: Harris discusses financial and property transfers in a long-term romantic relationship and warns against treating all such payments as necessarily taxable compensation or necessarily gifts. Specific payments for specified services may be different from support and gifts motivated by affection.
entries.source: Assigned 'Harris handout (2).pdf', scanned casebook excerpt, Chapter 3: The Private Sphere and the Public Sphere, printed pp. 154–161. Reference pages: 155–160.
entries.examApplication: Suppose one payment is tied to a specific contractual service and another is an unrestricted present motivated by personal affection. Identify donor intent separately for each transfer.
entries.examTrap: Neither 'romantic relationship' nor 'regular payment' alone supplies a conclusive answer.
entries.laymanExplanation: A friend sending birthday money is different from someone paying you to provide a service. The reason for the transfer matters more than its label.

entries.title: Criminal tax willfulness
entries.summary: A criminal tax conviction for willful nonpayment or nonfiling requires proof of a voluntary, intentional violation of a known legal duty.
entries.details: Harris involves §§7201 and 7203. In the criminal setting, the prosecution must prove the relevant criminal elements, including willfulness, beyond a reasonable doubt. A genuinely unsettled legal duty and a good-faith belief may defeat willfulness even if tax treatment could be contested in civil proceedings.
entries.source: Assigned 'Harris handout (2).pdf', scanned casebook excerpt, Chapter 3: The Private Sphere and the Public Sphere, printed pp. 154–161. Reference pages: 154–160.
entries.examApplication: Distinguish whether money is income for civil tax purposes from whether the recipient knowingly violated a clear legal duty and could be criminally convicted.
entries.examTrap: Uncertainty sufficient to prevent criminal conviction does not automatically mean the disputed receipt is an excluded gift.
entries.laymanExplanation: Criminal tax law generally requires more than a wrong return. The prosecution must prove the person intentionally violated a tax duty they knew they had.

entries.title: Criminal burden of proof versus civil tax determination
entries.summary: The government must establish the charged criminal tax offense beyond a reasonable doubt; civil taxability is a different question.
entries.details: In Harris, the court found the donor's purpose inadequately proved as to Conley and serious uncertainty about the tax classification as to Harris. The court stressed that the criminal law must provide fair warning before it may punish willful nonfiling or evasion.
entries.source: Assigned 'Harris handout (2).pdf', scanned casebook excerpt, Chapter 3: The Private Sphere and the Public Sphere, printed pp. 154–161. Reference pages: 154–160.
entries.examApplication: When a question asks whether a tax charge can support criminal sanctions, discuss donor intent, taxpayer knowledge, and legal clarity separately from the likely civil treatment.
entries.examTrap: Do not transform a reversal for insufficient criminal proof into a positive civil tax holding.
entries.laymanExplanation: A civil tax disagreement and a criminal tax prosecution have different stakes. Proving someone deliberately committed a crime is harder than disputing a tax bill.

entries.title: Letters offered to show belief, not necessarily their truth
entries.summary: A communication can be relevant to the recipient's state of mind without being offered as proof that its factual claims are true.
entries.details: Kritzik wrote Harris affectionate letters and described gifts. The court held the letters were relevant to Harris's good-faith belief about his purpose and therefore should not have been excluded as hearsay solely because the letters might be false. This is a supporting evidentiary point in the Tax opinion, not the central gift definition.
entries.source: Assigned 'Harris handout (2).pdf', scanned casebook excerpt, Chapter 3: The Private Sphere and the Public Sphere, printed pp. 154–161. Reference pages: 156–157.
entries.examApplication: A taxpayer's beliefs and the words communicated to them can matter to criminal willfulness, even when the exact objective truth of the statements is disputed.
entries.laymanExplanation: The donor wrote letters calling the transfers gifts. Even if those words were disputed, the recipient might reasonably believe them, which matters when deciding whether she knowingly committed a tax crime.

entries.title: United States v. Harris (7th Cir. 1991)
entries.summary: The Seventh Circuit reversed the convictions of Harris and Conley and ordered dismissal of their indictments; the government had not shown the criminal tax duty and willfulness needed for convictions.
entries.details: This is a reproduced judicial opinion in the assigned handout, not merely a citation. The handout also includes a separate concurrence by Judge Flaum expressing concern about an overly categorical approach to payments between romantic partners.
entries.source: Assigned 'Harris handout (2).pdf', scanned casebook excerpt, Chapter 3: The Private Sphere and the Public Sphere, printed pp. 154–161. Reproduced opinion 'United States v. Harris,' 942 F.2d 1125, at printed pp. 154–160; Judge Flaum's concurrence and notes through p. 161.
entries.facts: David Kritzik, a wealthy widower, gave Leigh Ann Conley and Lynnette Harris (twin sisters) substantial amounts of money and property during personal relationships. The government alleged they should have reported the transfers as taxable income; both were convicted in separate criminal trials. Conley's prosecution relied on inferences about the donor's intent. Harris attempted to introduce Kritzik's letters describing affection and gifts, but the district court excluded them.
entries.issue: Could the government sustain criminal tax convictions treating these transfers as taxable income when it had not proved donor intent, when Harris's evidence of her good-faith belief was excluded, and when relevant gift-versus-income law did not clearly establish criminal liability?
entries.holding: No. Conley's conviction was reversed because the government had not sufficiently shown Kritzik's intent and her knowledge. Harris's conviction was reversed because relevant letters should have been admitted to show good-faith belief and because the unclear tax law did not give fair warning sufficient for a willful criminal violation. The court ordered dismissal of both indictments.
entries.reasoning: Applying Duberstein, the court identified the transferor's intent as central to the gift inquiry. Gift-tax returns did not establish the nature of all transfers to Conley. For Harris, affectionate letters could affect her belief even if not true, and their exclusion denied evidence central to willfulness. Prior civil Tax Court cases indicated noncriminal gift treatment in comparable personal relationships; the law was too unclear for criminal sanctions. The opinion did not establish a categorical civil tax exemption for transfers between lovers. Judge Flaum concurred in the judgment but criticized the majority's broad language and favored case-by-case donor-intent analysis.
entries.rule: The §102(a) gift inquiry focuses on the transferor's motive under Duberstein; ambiguous civil tax classifications and failures to prove knowledge of a known duty can defeat criminal willfulness. Harris does not conclusively exempt all personal-relationship transfers from civil income tax.
entries.exam: When facing gifts-versus-income questions, analyze donor motive and any quid pro quo. If the hypothetical asks for criminal liability, separately analyze proof of willfulness and clarity of the legal duty. Do not equate absence of criminal liability with a holding that the amount was necessarily a civil-tax gift.
entries.examApplication: A wealthy individual gives recurring money and jewelry to a longtime romantic partner. Assess affection, potential payment for services, donor statements and gift returns. Then, if the recipient failed to file a return, explain why the government must independently show a known tax duty and intentional violation.

entries.title: IRC §1001 — realized gain or loss
entries.summary: Realized gain or loss generally equals amount realized minus adjusted basis.
entries.laymanExplanation: Sell an asset for $5,000 that has $1,000 basis: your realized gain is $4,000.

entries.title: IRC §1015(a) — gifted property generally takes donor's basis
entries.summary: A recipient of gifted property generally takes the donor's adjusted basis to determine gain on a later disposition.
entries.laymanExplanation: Giving your child stock doesn't erase the profit already built into it. Your child usually inherits your tax cost.
entries.legalExplanation: Under §1015(a), the donee typically assumes donor's adjusted basis; the donor's untaxed appreciation remains built in. A special dual-basis limitation applies when FMV at gift is below donor's basis, for determining losses.

entries.title: IRC §1015(a) — dual basis for gifts of loss property
entries.summary: If donor basis exceeds FMV when gifted, donee generally uses donor basis for gain and gift-date FMV for loss.
entries.laymanExplanation: If someone gives you a stock they bought for $2,000 when it's worth only $1,000, you can't claim the donor's full old loss if you sell it for $500.
entries.legalExplanation: The statute prevents shifting built-in loss to the donee. If sale price exceeds donor basis, use donor basis for gain; if it falls below gift-date FMV, use gift-date FMV for loss; if sale proceeds lie between those figures, generally no recognized gain or loss from the basis comparison.

entries.title: Transferred (carryover) basis versus substituted basis
entries.summary: Transferred basis follows the property's former owner's basis; substituted basis derives from basis in another asset or event under statutory rules.
entries.laymanExplanation: A gift recipient generally starts with the donor's tax cost, not today's market price.
entries.legalExplanation: The source distinguishes 'transferred basis' under §7701(a)(43) from 'exchanged/substituted basis' terminology under §7701(a)(42)-(44); practitioners often use 'carryover' broadly. By contrast, §1014 generally resets basis on qualifying property acquired from a decedent.

entries.title: Fair market value on the gift date

entries.legalExplanation: For purposes of §1015(a)'s loss-basis limitation, gift-date FMV serves as the loss basis if it is below donor basis; valuation is not a new fair-market-value gain basis. The chapter questions require checking each potential sale price.

entries.title: Built-in gain and built-in loss

entries.legalExplanation: Gifted property with built-in appreciation generally preserves the gain through donor carryover basis. A built-in loss is subject to the distinct FMV-limited loss basis, which prevents loss shifting by gift.

entries.title: IRC §1015(d) — basis adjustment for gift tax paid
entries.summary: Certain federal gift tax paid by the donor can increase a donee's basis, with statutory limits for post-1976 gifts.
entries.laymanExplanation: If the giver actually pays gift tax, part of that tax can sometimes raise the recipient's basis.
entries.legalExplanation: The notes identify §1015(d) and its limitation for gifts made after 1977 to gift tax attributable to net appreciation. This is a narrow calculation overlay, not a blanket addition of the entire gift tax.

entries.title: IRC §1014 — basis of inherited property
entries.summary: Qualifying property acquired from a decedent generally receives a basis equal to date-of-death FMV or an eligible alternate valuation date.
entries.laymanExplanation: If an heir receives stock worth $500,000 that the decedent bought for $50,000, the heir's starting basis may be about $500,000, subject to statutory exceptions.
entries.legalExplanation: Under §1014 and qualifying estate valuation rules, basis generally steps up or down to FMV at death (or alternate date elected under §2032), often removing previously unrealized appreciation from future income tax. Some property and income-in-respect-of-decedent categories have exceptions.

entries.title: Lock-in effect and buy-borrow-die

entries.laymanExplanation: Selling appreciated stock may trigger gains tax, so wealthy owners can keep it, borrow against it, and pass it on instead.
entries.legalExplanation: The notes discuss incentives created by §1014 and borrowing against appreciated assets. Loans usually do not themselves create income due to a repayment obligation; holding assets until death can avoid realization before the basis adjustment, subject to tax-law exceptions and financing risks.

entries.title: Taft v. Bowers
entries.summary: The Supreme Court sustained the statutory rule taxing a donee on gain measured from the donor's cost basis, including appreciation predating the gift.
entries.laymanExplanation: A father bought stock for $1,000, gifted it when worth $2,000, and the recipient sold it for $5,000. The recipient's gain was $4,000, not just the last $3,000 of growth.
entries.legalExplanation: Opinion reproduced in assigned Chapter 3 pp135–137.
entries.details: Opinion reproduced in assigned Chapter 3 pp135–137.
entries.source: Bankman et al. (19th ed.), Week 4 assigned printed pp. 135–137.
entries.facts: A bought 100 shares of stock for $1,000; by the time he gifted them to B they were worth $2,000. B later sold the stock for $5,000. The tax statute applied A's original cost basis to B; B asserted the first $1,000 of appreciation occurred while A owned it and therefore could not be taxed to B.
entries.issue: Can Congress constitutionally tax the donee on the entire gain measured from the donor's basis, including appreciation during the donor's ownership?
entries.holding: Yes. The Court affirmed that the donee owed tax on $4,000 total realized gain after a $5,000 sale using the original $1,000 basis.
entries.reasoning: The property represented one original capital investment by the donor. The appreciation was not taxed at the moment of gift, but became realized on the donee's later sale. Congress could make a succeeding owner assume the predecessor's tax position; the Sixteenth Amendment did not bar the carryover-basis scheme.
entries.rule: A donee who later sells gifted appreciated property can be taxed on the total appreciation measured against the donor's original basis, not merely the period after receipt.
entries.exam: Compute transferred basis and gain under §1015/§1001. Contrast §1014 at death and the special loss-basis limitation for depreciated gifts.
entries.examApplication: Gift FMV $2,000; donor basis $1,000; donee sale $5,000 -> $4,000 gain.
entries.examTrap: The fact that a gift is excluded under §102 does NOT eliminate the pre-gift appreciation when a donee sells.

entries.title: IRC §1041 — spousal and divorce-related property transfers
entries.summary: No gain or loss generally is recognized on property transfers between spouses or former spouses incident to divorce.
entries.laymanExplanation: If one spouse transfers appreciated shares to the other as part of divorce, the person giving them usually doesn't pay gains tax at that moment.
entries.legalExplanation: Section 1041(a) generally provides nonrecognition for transfers between spouses and former spouses incident to divorce. Section 1041(b) treats the recipient as receiving property by gift and taking transferor's adjusted basis. This was Congress's statutory response to United States v. entries.title: IRC §1041(b) — transferee carries over basis
entries.summary: A qualifying recipient spouse generally gets the transferor's adjusted basis instead of fair market value.
entries.laymanExplanation: Receiving $500,000 worth of stock with $50,000 basis doesn't automatically give the recipient $500,000 of new basis.
entries.legalExplanation: Nonrecognition means unrecognized built-in gain or loss persists after transfer. Under §1041(b), the recipient is treated as acquiring the property by gift and receives transferor's adjusted basis, even though the property may be awarded in a contested separation.

entries.title: Release of marital rights as consideration

entries.laymanExplanation: Before today's nonrecognition statute, trading appreciated shares for a spouse's release of property claims could trigger tax.
entries.legalExplanation: Davis treated the husband's transfer of appreciated stock in satisfaction of the wife's inchoate rights under Delaware law as a taxable exchange. Where no direct valuation existed, the Court presumed arm's-length exchanged values to equal the FMV of property transferred. §1041 later superseded the recognition rule for covered transfers.

This is historical case analysis, not today's general spousal-transfer recognition rule.

entries.summary: Prior law made divorce settlements difficult to value and taxed couples differently depending on state marital-property rules.

entries.legalExplanation: Davis created disputes over whether marital rights were ownership or obligations and their market value. Modern §1041 offers nonrecognition and transferred basis for qualifying transfers; historical case opinions remain important for understanding the policy shift.

entries.title: United States v. Davis
entries.summary: Under pre-§1041 law, the Supreme Court treated a husband's stock transfer to his former wife for release of marital rights as a taxable exchange, with gain measured using FMV.
entries.laymanExplanation: A husband gave appreciated DuPont stock to settle divorce rights. The Supreme Court treated it like a sale that could create taxable profit—but Congress later changed the rule.
entries.legalExplanation: The opinion is reproduced in the assigned pages; its taxable-exchange result is historically superseded for qualifying transfers by §1041.
entries.details: The opinion is reproduced in the assigned pages; its taxable-exchange result is historically superseded for qualifying transfers by §1041.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., Week 4 assigned printed pp. 142–146
entries.facts: Thomas Crawley Davis conveyed 1,000 shares of appreciated DuPont stock under a Delaware separation agreement to settle his wife's marital rights. Under state law, the wife had inchoate rights and possible future marital claims but did not hold an ownership interest identical to community property.
entries.issue: Did the husband's stock transfer in settlement of marital rights realize taxable gain, and could the released rights be valued?
entries.holding: The Supreme Court held the transfer was a taxable exchange under the law then in force; the value of marital rights received was reasonably measured by the FMV of stock transferred, and the husband's gain was taxable.
entries.reasoning: Delaware law gave the wife burdens and claims against the husband's property, not the kind of co-ownership making it a mere division of existing property. The court assumed arm's-length equal values in settlement, enabling the amount realized under §1001 to be measured by stock FMV. It sought consistency in taxing growth in appreciated assets when exchanged for valuable rights.
entries.rule: Historical holding: exchange of appreciated property for release of marital rights could cause realization and recognition of gain, measured by FMV of property transferred; §1041 later governs qualifying transactions instead.
entries.exam: First use current §1041 for qualifying spouse/former-spouse incident-to-divorce transfers. If analyzing Davis, identify it as pre-§1041 historical doctrine and explain why the statute replaced the result.
entries.examApplication: Husband transfers $100,000-FMV stock with $40,000 basis in divorce settlement. Under historical Davis exchange, $60,000 realized gain; if §1041 applies, no current gain recognized and spouse carries $40,000 basis.
entries.examTrap: Do not use Davis's historical taxable-exchange holding as controlling for current qualifying §1041 divorce transfers.

entries.title: Farid-Es-Sultaneh v. Commissioner
entries.summary: The court held an antenuptial stock transfer for release of substantial marital rights was a purchase for income-tax basis, not automatically a gift governed by donor carryover basis.
entries.laymanExplanation: Before a marriage, a wealthy man gave stock in return for his future wife's agreement to give up valuable marital claims. The court treated her as having paid with rights rather than getting a free gift.
entries.legalExplanation: The reproduced assigned opinion distinguishes §1012 cost basis from §1015 gift basis and gift-tax definitions.
entries.details: The reproduced assigned opinion distinguishes §1012 cost basis from §1015 gift basis and gift-tax definitions.
entries.source: Bankman et al., 19th ed., Week 4 assigned printed pp. 147–150
entries.facts: In 1924, S.S. Kresge transferred to his future spouse Farid-Es-Sultaneh shares worth about $800,000 as part of an antenuptial arrangement; she agreed to marry and relinquish support, dower and other valuable marital rights. His basis was about 15 cents per share, FMV near $10 per share at transfer; she later sold part at $19 per share. IRS treated the shares as gifts with donor basis; the Tax Court agreed.
entries.issue: Was the stock received as a §1015 gift using Kresge's low basis, or acquired for fair consideration under an antenuptial agreement and therefore cost basis?
entries.holding: The Second Circuit reversed: the transfer was supported by valuable consideration consisting of marital rights released, making her a purchaser rather than donee for income-tax basis purposes.
entries.reasoning: Income-tax classification does not automatically import estate/gift tax's specialized restrictions on marital-right consideration. The antenuptial contract represented real exchange for valuable rights, and the Court found that the shares were not a completed unconditional gift before the agreement.
entries.rule: For income-tax purposes, a stock transfer in exchange for adequate consideration is not necessarily a §1015 gift merely because gift-tax statutes or the parties' documents call it a gift; historical application required a cost-basis analysis.
entries.exam: Distinguish §1012 cost basis and §1015 carryover basis, classify transfer timing, determine whether §1041 covers the facts and separate income-tax from gift-tax standards.
entries.examApplication: A prospective spouse gives stock in exchange for releasing enforceable marital rights before marriage. Evaluate exchange/consideration and whether current §1041 actually applies.
entries.examTrap: Do not assume all prenups are gifts or automatically protected by §1041 before the parties are married.

entries.title: Diez-Arguelles v. Commissioner
entries.summary: The Tax Court rejected a bad-debt deduction for unpaid child support because the parent had no tax basis in the unpaid obligation.
entries.laymanExplanation: A parent never received the child support her ex-husband legally owed. The court said that missing money was not a deductible bad debt because she had no tax basis in it.
entries.legalExplanation: Opinion excerpt reproduced in assigned Chapter 3 pp151–152.
entries.details: Opinion excerpt reproduced in assigned Chapter 3 pp151–152.
entries.source: Bankman et al., Federal Income Taxation (19th ed.), Week 4 assigned pp. 151–152
entries.facts: Christina Diez-Arguelles divorced Kevin Baxter and was owed $300 monthly child support. He failed to make payments, leaving $4,325 arrears through 1978 and another $3,000 in 1979. Christina and her husband supported the children themselves and claimed the unpaid sums as bad-debt losses, despite repeated unsuccessful collection attempts and court orders.
entries.issue: Could the custodial parent deduct unpaid child-support arrears as nonbusiness bad debts under §166(d) despite having no tax basis in the expected support payments?
entries.holding: No. The Tax Court rejected the deductions because the taxpayer had no basis in the overdue child-support obligations.
entries.reasoning: A nonbusiness bad-debt deduction under §166(d) also requires adjusted basis under §166(b). The taxpayer did not loan money to Baxter or include the promised child-support amounts in taxable income and could not create basis merely by paying the children's ongoing household expenses. A state court judgment did not by itself establish a federal tax basis.
entries.rule: Nonbusiness bad-debt loss deductions require actual adjusted basis in the debt; unreceived child-support obligations cannot be deducted merely because they are legally owed and uncollectible.
entries.exam: Identify a debt, whether it became wholly worthless, and importantly whether the claimant has adjusted basis. Distinguish a loaned and later defaulted amount from unreceived personal-support payments.
entries.examApplication: Parent is owed $7,325 in past-due child support and has no basis in the claim: §166(d) generally provides no deduction for the unpaid amount.
entries.examTrap: A court order and actual household expenses do not automatically create basis in unpaid child support.

entries.laymanExplanation: Paying the same tax next year is usually better than paying it now because you can use today's money meanwhile.

entries.title: Burnet v. Sanford & Brooks Co.
entries.summary: No. The Supreme Court held the business recovery and interest taxable as gross income in 1920 under the annual accounting regime.
entries.laymanExplanation: A dredging company lost money over several years, then won repayment from the government. The Court said the repayment counts in the year received, not by adding every year of the project together.
entries.details: This judicial opinion is reproduced in the assigned textbook excerpt.
entries.facts: A dredging contractor incurred expenses exceeding payments during a dredging project performed 1913–1915, then sued for breach of contract. In 1920 it recovered $192,577.59 including $176,271.88 compensating previously deducted operating expenses and $16,305.71 interest. It sought to exclude the expense reimbursement because the entire contract ultimately generated no net profit.
entries.issue: May the taxpayer exclude recovery of previously expensed business costs in 1920 because the underlying multiyear contract produced no overall profit?
entries.holding: No. The Supreme Court held the business recovery and interest taxable as gross income in 1920 under the annual accounting regime.
entries.reasoning: Annual returns determine income for fixed periods. Operating expenses deducted in earlier years were not capital invested in property. Congress could tax later-year recoveries notwithstanding prior losses and the transaction's ultimate poor outcome; a lifetime transaction-wide system was not constitutionally required.
entries.rule: Taxable income is generally computed by taxable year; a later recovery of earlier business costs can be gross income even where the entire transaction is unprofitable.

entries.title: Georgia School-Book Depository v. Commissioner
entries.summary: The Tax Court required commissions earned from state-book transactions to be included when the right to payment accrued, despite delay in collection.
entries.laymanExplanation: A textbook broker earned commissions but waited for Georgia to pay. The court said the commissions were already earned, even though cash had not arrived.
entries.details: This judicial opinion is reproduced in the assigned textbook excerpt.
entries.facts: An accrual-basis broker earned 8% commissions arranging, warehousing and distributing schoolbooks for Georgia schools. The state textbook fund, fed by beer excise tax, was short and paid later. The broker reported commissions on state books only when the state settled, though it accrued other book commissions sooner.
entries.issue: Did the commissions accrue when brokerage work was performed or only when the state later paid?
entries.holding: The Tax Court required commissions earned from state-book transactions to be included when the right to payment accrued, despite delay in collection.
entries.reasoning: Substantially all services were completed and entitlement fixed. Delay or lack of current funds did not demonstrate an unresolved condition or reasonable certainty of permanent nonpayment; the state's resources and improving collections supported expected ultimate payment. Broad exceptions would let taxpayers arbitrarily shift years.
entries.rule: Under the accrual method, a fixed, earned right to be paid generally creates income even when payment is delayed. Genuine contingency or proven uncollectibility may justify exception.
entries.exam: Separate whether work has earned the fee (right fixed) from whether the payor is merely late. Compare Hallmark's retention of title (cited in note, not independently reproduced).

entries.title: American Automobile Association v. United States
entries.summary: No. The Court affirmed rejection of the proration and required advance dues to be included in the year received under the applicable law and facts.
entries.laymanExplanation: An auto club took a year's membership fee upfront and wanted to spread income across the months. The Supreme Court let the IRS require it all to be counted when received.
entries.details: This judicial opinion is reproduced in the assigned textbook excerpt.
entries.facts: AAA, an accrual-basis auto club, received prepaid annual dues for road services provided on demand. It recognized dues ratably across the membership term under GAAP and reserved portions for next year. IRS under §446(b) required inclusion of dues in the year received, denying deferral for expected future service costs.
entries.issue: Did AAA's GAAP-consistent ratable method clearly reflect taxable income so IRS was bound to accept it?
entries.holding: No. The Court affirmed rejection of the proration and required advance dues to be included in the year received under the applicable law and facts.
entries.reasoning: Member services were contingent on future demand rather than scheduled specific obligations, and average service estimates did not fix the actual earning of each payment. Legislative context included repeal of permissive deferred-revenue provisions and limited subscriber provisions. Justice Stewart dissented, defending matching and reliable aggregate accounting.
entries.rule: Under the law then applicable, the IRS could reject AAA's deferred reporting of on-demand prepaid dues even when the taxpayer's financial books reasonably spread them over the service period.

entries.title: Eisner v. Macomber
entries.summary: No. The Supreme Court held that the pro rata distribution did not constitute realized shareholder income on those facts and could not be taxed as income in that manner.
entries.laymanExplanation: The company gave every shareholder more shares in proportion to what they already held. Nobody got a bigger piece of the company, so the Court said this stock dividend wasn't income.
entries.details: This judicial opinion is reproduced in the assigned textbook excerpt.
entries.facts: Macomber held common stock in Standard Oil of California. The corporation issued a pro rata common-stock dividend from accumulated profits, increasing her number of shares but leaving her fractional ownership basically unchanged. The government sought income tax based on a portion of the new shares' par value.
entries.issue: Did a pro rata stock dividend constitute 'income' taxable without apportionment under the Sixteenth Amendment?
entries.holding: No. The Supreme Court held that the pro rata distribution did not constitute realized shareholder income on those facts and could not be taxed as income in that manner.
entries.reasoning: The shareholder had not received assets severed from corporate capital and her proportional ownership remained the same. The Court emphasized realization and distinguished capital from income; dissenting opinions challenged the narrow constitutional conclusion. Subsequent law and §§305–307 address stock dividends, while Glenshaw Glass rejected Macomber's narrow phrase as a complete definition of income.
entries.rule: On its facts, a pure pro rata stock dividend leaving shareholder's substantive ownership unchanged was not a realization of income; later statutory and judicial law constrain broad readings of the opinion.
entries.exam: Check whether the distribution changes shareholders' proportions, gives an election of cash, or qualifies under §305 and exceptions; do not rely on the old capital/labor formulation.

entries.examTrap: Do not cite Macomber as a universal constitutional prohibition on taxing every unrealized gain. Glenshaw Glass displaced its narrow definition and later cases address realization.
